frontHtml: Antibody deficiencies: B-cell development, class switching and plasma-cell output: They share one infection pattern: […] ( Streptococcus pneumoniae , nontypeable and type b Haemophilus influenzae ), plus a few organisms that antibody normally neutralises at mucosal or bloodstream stages: enteroviruses and Giardia .
backHtml: They share one infection pattern: recurrent sinopulmonary infection with encapsulated, extracellular bacteria ( Streptococcus pneumoniae , nontypeable and type b Haemophilus influenzae ), plus a few organisms that antibody normally neutralises at mucosal or bloodstream stages: enteroviruses and Giardia .

frontHtml: Antibody deficiencies: B-cell development, class switching and plasma-cell output: Two infections are characteristic: […] (echovirus, coxsackievirus), a slowly progressive encephalitis that reflects the central role of neutralising antibody in enterovirus clearance, and vaccine-associated paralytic polio after live oral polio vaccine.
backHtml: Two infections are characteristic: chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis (echovirus, coxsackievirus), a slowly progressive encephalitis that reflects the central role of neutralising antibody in enterovirus clearance, and vaccine-associated paralytic polio after live oral polio vaccine.

frontHtml: Antibody deficiencies: B-cell development, class switching and plasma-cell output: B cells are present in most patients, often with reduced class-switched memory B cells, so the lesion is a failure of […] rather than absent B cells.
backHtml: B cells are present in most patients, often with reduced class-switched memory B cells, so the lesion is a failure of terminal differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells rather than absent B cells.

frontHtml: Severe combined immunodeficiency and 22q11.2 deletion: failures of T-cell development: Omenn syndrome results from hypomorphic (leaky) mutations, most often in […].
backHtml: Omenn syndrome results from hypomorphic (leaky) mutations, most often in RAG1 / RAG2.

frontHtml: Severe combined immunodeficiency and 22q11.2 deletion: failures of T-cell development: They do not replicate, so their number in a dried blood spot reflects […].
backHtml: They do not replicate, so their number in a dried blood spot reflects recent thymic output.

frontHtml: Severe combined immunodeficiency and 22q11.2 deletion: failures of T-cell development: Hemizygous deletion of about 3 Mb including […] disturbs development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and the outflow tract.
backHtml: Hemizygous deletion of about 3 Mb including TBX1 disturbs development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches and the outflow tract.

frontHtml: Syndromic and pathway-specific T-cell defects: WAS, A-T, IL-12/IFN-γ, Th17 and hyper-IgE: X-linked loss of WAS protein, a hematopoietic regulator of […] downstream of receptor signalling.
backHtml: X-linked loss of WAS protein, a hematopoietic regulator of actin polymerisation downstream of receptor signalling.

frontHtml: Syndromic and pathway-specific T-cell defects: WAS, A-T, IL-12/IFN-γ, Th17 and hyper-IgE: Autosomal recessive loss of […], a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and activates p53, checkpoint kinase 2 and repair.
backHtml: Autosomal recessive loss of ATM, a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and activates p53, checkpoint kinase 2 and repair.

frontHtml: Syndromic and pathway-specific T-cell defects: WAS, A-T, IL-12/IFN-γ, Th17 and hyper-IgE: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) : most often due to […] mutations, which tilt signalling away from Th17 development; also IL-17RA, IL-17F and RORC defects.
backHtml: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) : most often due to STAT1 gain-of-function mutations, which tilt signalling away from Th17 development; also IL-17RA, IL-17F and RORC defects.

frontHtml: Syndromic and pathway-specific T-cell defects: WAS, A-T, IL-12/IFN-γ, Th17 and hyper-IgE: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome : dominant-negative […] mutations block IL-6 and IL-23 signalling and so Th17 differentiation.
backHtml: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome : dominant-negative STAT3 mutations block IL-6 and IL-23 signalling and so Th17 differentiation.

frontHtml: Complement deficiencies: pathway, regulator and drug-induced: The risk of an […] is graded by how early the block is: almost all people with complete C1q deficiency develop it, most with C4 deficiency, and a smaller fraction with C2 deficiency.
backHtml: The risk of an SLE-like illness is graded by how early the block is: almost all people with complete C1q deficiency develop it, most with C4 deficiency, and a smaller fraction with C2 deficiency.

frontHtml: Complement deficiencies: pathway, regulator and drug-induced: Bradykinin acting on endothelial B2 receptors widens interendothelial gaps, producing deep, non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling of skin, gut wall and larynx lasting 2–5 days, […], and resistant to antihistamines, glucocorticoids and epinephrine.
backHtml: Bradykinin acting on endothelial B2 receptors widens interendothelial gaps, producing deep, non-pitting, non-pruritic swelling of skin, gut wall and larynx lasting 2–5 days, without urticaria, and resistant to antihistamines, glucocorticoids and epinephrine.

frontHtml: Complement deficiencies: pathway, regulator and drug-induced: In both, […], even between attacks in most patients, while C1q is normal .
backHtml: In both, C4 is low, even between attacks in most patients, while C1q is normal .

frontHtml: Phagocyte and NK-cell defects: production, adhesion, granules, killing and cytotoxicity: The classic teaching is that catalase-negative bacteria leak their own H 2 O 2 into the phagosome and are killed with the host's myeloperoxidase, whereas […] degrade it and survive.
backHtml: The classic teaching is that catalase-negative bacteria leak their own H 2 O 2 into the phagosome and are killed with the host's myeloperoxidase, whereas catalase-producing organisms degrade it and survive.

frontHtml: Phagocyte and NK-cell defects: production, adhesion, granules, killing and cytotoxicity: Most patients without transplantation enter an […], which is hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is the most frequent inherited phagocyte defect; it is usually asymptomatic because the oxidative burst still kills, but some patients, especially those with diabetes, develop invasive candidiasis.
backHtml: Most patients without transplantation enter an accelerated phase, which is hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is the most frequent inherited phagocyte defect; it is usually asymptomatic because the oxidative burst still kills, but some patients, especially those with diabetes, develop invasive candidiasis.

frontHtml: Phagocyte and NK-cell defects: production, adhesion, granules, killing and cytotoxicity: The marrow shows […].
backHtml: The marrow shows maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage.

frontHtml: Phagocyte and NK-cell defects: production, adhesion, granules, killing and cytotoxicity: In […], cytotoxic T and NK cells recognise their target but cannot kill it, so the target cell (often an infected antigen-presenting cell) persists and keeps stimulating them.
backHtml: In familial HLH, cytotoxic T and NK cells recognise their target but cannot kill it, so the target cell (often an infected antigen-presenting cell) persists and keeps stimulating them.

frontHtml: Recurrent infections and antibody deficiency: workup and IgG replacement: Specific antibody testing is essential when IgG is only modestly low or normal; it must be done […], because infused IgG contains these antibodies and makes results uninterpretable.
backHtml: Specific antibody testing is essential when IgG is only modestly low or normal; it must be done before IgG replacement, because infused IgG contains these antibodies and makes results uninterpretable.

frontHtml: Recurrent infections and antibody deficiency: workup and IgG replacement: The starting dose for primary antibody deficiency is about […] per 4 weeks, adjusted to clinical response rather than to a single trough target; patients with bronchiectasis usually need higher troughs.
backHtml: The starting dose for primary antibody deficiency is about 400–600 mg/kg per 4 weeks, adjusted to clinical response rather than to a single trough target; patients with bronchiectasis usually need higher troughs.

frontHtml: Recurrent infections and antibody deficiency: workup and IgG replacement: In selective IgA deficiency with a history of anaphylaxis to blood products and anti-IgA antibodies, give […] and plasma from IgA-deficient donors ; for future elective needs, consider autologous donation.
backHtml: In selective IgA deficiency with a history of anaphylaxis to blood products and anti-IgA antibodies, give washed red cells or platelets and plasma from IgA-deficient donors ; for future elective needs, consider autologous donation.

frontHtml: Cellular and combined immunodeficiency: newborn screening, protection and definitive therapy: An absent or low TREC result is followed by […] on peripheral blood: CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 or CD20, CD16/56, and the naive T-cell marker CD45RA, with T-cell proliferation to mitogens when T cells are present.
backHtml: An absent or low TREC result is followed by lymphocyte flow cytometry on peripheral blood: CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 or CD20, CD16/56, and the naive T-cell marker CD45RA, with T-cell proliferation to mitogens when T cells are present.

frontHtml: Cellular and combined immunodeficiency: newborn screening, protection and definitive therapy: For ADA-SCID, […] stabilises the infant until transplantation, and autologous gene therapy is an established alternative at specialist centres.
backHtml: For ADA-SCID, PEG-conjugated ADA enzyme replacement (elapegademase) stabilises the infant until transplantation, and autologous gene therapy is an established alternative at specialist centres.

frontHtml: Cellular and combined immunodeficiency: newborn screening, protection and definitive therapy: A raised […] after the first year of life is the most useful first test; genetic testing of ATM confirms it.
backHtml: A raised serum α-fetoprotein after the first year of life is the most useful first test; genetic testing of ATM confirms it.

frontHtml: Complement deficiency, hereditary angioedema and C5 inhibitors: testing and treatment: Test with […] (classical pathway lytic function) and AH50 (alternative pathway), plus C3 and C4.
backHtml: Test with CH50 (classical pathway lytic function) and AH50 (alternative pathway), plus C3 and C4.

frontHtml: Complement deficiency, hereditary angioedema and C5 inhibitors: testing and treatment: Terminal component, properdin, C3, factor H or factor I deficiency: […] and serogroup B (MenB) vaccines with booster doses while risk persists, plus pneumococcal and H. influenzae type b vaccination.
backHtml: Terminal component, properdin, C3, factor H or factor I deficiency: quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate (MenACWY) and serogroup B (MenB) vaccines with booster doses while risk persists, plus pneumococcal and H. influenzae type b vaccination.

frontHtml: Complement deficiency, hereditary angioedema and C5 inhibitors: testing and treatment: Avoid […] and hormone therapy and ACE inhibitors ; progestin-only methods are acceptable.
backHtml: Avoid estrogen-containing contraceptives and hormone therapy and ACE inhibitors ; progestin-only methods are acceptable.

frontHtml: Complement deficiency, hereditary angioedema and C5 inhibitors: testing and treatment: Give […] vaccines at least 2 weeks before the first dose; if treatment cannot wait, start the drug with antibacterial prophylaxis until 2 weeks after vaccination.
backHtml: Give MenACWY and MenB vaccines at least 2 weeks before the first dose; if treatment cannot wait, start the drug with antibacterial prophylaxis until 2 weeks after vaccination.

frontHtml: Phagocyte, neutropenia, NK and HLH disorders: diagnosis and management: Confirm by […] on leukocytes (CD15s, sialyl Lewis X, for LAD-2).
backHtml: Confirm by flow cytometry for CD18 and CD11 expression on leukocytes (CD15s, sialyl Lewis X, for LAD-2).

frontHtml: Phagocyte, neutropenia, NK and HLH disorders: diagnosis and management: Severe LAD-1 is fatal in childhood without […]; milder forms are managed with meticulous dental care and prompt, prolonged antibiotics.
backHtml: Severe LAD-1 is fatal in childhood without hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; milder forms are managed with meticulous dental care and prompt, prolonged antibiotics.

frontHtml: Phagocyte, neutropenia, NK and HLH disorders: diagnosis and management: Treatment : daily subcutaneous […], titrated to an ANC that prevents infection; most patients respond.
backHtml: Treatment : daily subcutaneous G-CSF (filgrastim), titrated to an ANC that prevents infection; most patients respond.

frontHtml: Phagocyte, neutropenia, NK and HLH disorders: diagnosis and management: Flow cytometry (CD16/CD56 subsets) and NK cytotoxicity assays guide diagnosis. GATA2 deficiency (monocytopenia, B and NK lymphopenia, disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria, HPV, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis) carries a high lifetime risk of […]; marrow surveillance and early transplantation are standard.
backHtml: Flow cytometry (CD16/CD56 subsets) and NK cytotoxicity assays guide diagnosis. GATA2 deficiency (monocytopenia, B and NK lymphopenia, disseminated nontuberculous mycobacteria, HPV, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis) carries a high lifetime risk of myelodysplasia and AML; marrow surveillance and early transplantation are standard.

frontHtml: HIV-1 and HIV-2: virology, life cycle and immunopathogenesis: Each virion carries […] plus three enzymes packaged from the pol gene: reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease.
backHtml: Each virion carries two copies of positive-sense single-stranded RNA plus three enzymes packaged from the pol gene: reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease.

frontHtml: HIV-1 and HIV-2: virology, life cycle and immunopathogenesis: Coreceptor binding. A conformational change exposes a site for a chemokine receptor: […] (R5 virus, predominant early in infection and transmitted between people) or CXCR4 (X4 virus, which emerges later in some patients and is linked to faster CD4 loss).
backHtml: Coreceptor binding. A conformational change exposes a site for a chemokine receptor: CCR5 (R5 virus, predominant early in infection and transmitted between people) or CXCR4 (X4 virus, which emerges later in some patients and is linked to faster CD4 loss).

frontHtml: HIV-1 and HIV-2: virology, life cycle and immunopathogenesis: It is […] and to enfuvirtide, and some protease inhibitors are less active; INSTIs and NRTIs work.
backHtml: It is intrinsically resistant to NNRTIs and to enfuvirtide, and some protease inhibitors are less active; INSTIs and NRTIs work.

frontHtml: Antiretroviral pharmacology and HIV-associated organ disease: Kaposi sarcoma is an endothelial-derived tumor driven by […] (KSHV).
backHtml: Kaposi sarcoma is an endothelial-derived tumor driven by human herpesvirus 8 (KSHV).

frontHtml: Antiretroviral pharmacology and HIV-associated organ disease: Histology shows […] with extravasated red cells and hemosiderin; HHV-8 LANA immunostaining confirms it.
backHtml: Histology shows spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated red cells and hemosiderin; HHV-8 LANA immunostaining confirms it.

frontHtml: Antiretroviral pharmacology and HIV-associated organ disease: Biopsy shows […] with hypertrophied podocytes and microcystic tubular dilation.
backHtml: Biopsy shows collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis with hypertrophied podocytes and microcystic tubular dilation.

frontHtml: Antiretroviral pharmacology and HIV-associated organ disease: Pathology shows microglial nodules and […] (fused infected macrophages), because neurons themselves are not infected.
backHtml: Pathology shows microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells (fused infected macrophages), because neurons themselves are not infected.

frontHtml: Hypersensitivity types I–IV: mechanisms and prototypes: IL-4 and IL-13 drive B-cell class switching to IgE ; IgE binds the high-affinity receptor […] on mast cells and basophils. Re-exposure: a multivalent allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules, triggering degranulation.
backHtml: IL-4 and IL-13 drive B-cell class switching to IgE ; IgE binds the high-affinity receptor FcεRI on mast cells and basophils. Re-exposure: a multivalent allergen cross-links adjacent IgE molecules, triggering degranulation.

frontHtml: Hypersensitivity types I–IV: mechanisms and prototypes: The […], hours later, is driven by recruited eosinophils (IL-5), Th2 cells and basophils and explains recurrent wheeze after allergen exposure.
backHtml: The late phase, hours later, is driven by recruited eosinophils (IL-5), Th2 cells and basophils and explains recurrent wheeze after allergen exposure.

frontHtml: Hypersensitivity types I–IV: mechanisms and prototypes: The […] is the local form: in a person with high levels of preformed IgG, injected antigen (classically a too-frequent tetanus-diphtheria booster) forms complexes in the dermis, producing a painful, swollen, sometimes necrotic area 4–12 hours later. Serum sickness is the systemic form, appearing 1–2 weeks after a foreign protein (antivenom, antithymocyte globulin, chimeric antibodies) with fever, urticarial or purpuric rash, arthralgia and sometimes proteinuria.
backHtml: The Arthus reaction is the local form: in a person with high levels of preformed IgG, injected antigen (classically a too-frequent tetanus-diphtheria booster) forms complexes in the dermis, producing a painful, swollen, sometimes necrotic area 4–12 hours later. Serum sickness is the systemic form, appearing 1–2 weeks after a foreign protein (antivenom, antithymocyte globulin, chimeric antibodies) with fever, urticarial or purpuric rash, arthralgia and sometimes proteinuria.

frontHtml: Hypersensitivity types I–IV: mechanisms and prototypes: In the […], memory Th1 cells recognize mycobacterial peptides on dermal antigen-presenting cells and secrete IFN-γ, which activates macrophages; the result is induration peaking at 48–72 hours.
backHtml: In the tuberculin reaction, memory Th1 cells recognize mycobacterial peptides on dermal antigen-presenting cells and secrete IFN-γ, which activates macrophages; the result is induration peaking at 48–72 hours.

frontHtml: Transplant immunology: HLA, rejection and graft-versus-host disease: The main barrier to transplantation is the […], called HLA in humans and encoded on the short arm of chromosome 6.
backHtml: The main barrier to transplantation is the major histocompatibility complex, called HLA in humans and encoded on the short arm of chromosome 6.

frontHtml: Transplant immunology: HLA, rejection and graft-versus-host disease: GVHD occurs when […] enter a host who cannot reject them and who expresses foreign HLA.
backHtml: GVHD occurs when immunocompetent donor T cells enter a host who cannot reject them and who expresses foreign HLA.

frontHtml: Transplant immunology: HLA, rejection and graft-versus-host disease: Transfusion-associated GVHD appears 1–2 weeks after transfusion with fever, rash, diarrhea, liver injury and, unlike stem cell GVHD, […], because the host marrow itself is the target.
backHtml: Transfusion-associated GVHD appears 1–2 weeks after transfusion with fever, rash, diarrhea, liver injury and, unlike stem cell GVHD, marrow aplasia with pancytopenia, because the host marrow itself is the target.

frontHtml: Immunosuppressive drugs: mechanisms and toxicities: T-cell activation needs three signals: antigen on MHC binding the T-cell receptor (signal 1), costimulation through […] (signal 2), and IL-2 acting through its receptor to drive proliferation (signal 3).
backHtml: T-cell activation needs three signals: antigen on MHC binding the T-cell receptor (signal 1), costimulation through CD28 binding B7 (CD80/CD86) (signal 2), and IL-2 acting through its receptor to drive proliferation (signal 3).

frontHtml: Immunosuppressive drugs: mechanisms and toxicities: Lymphocytes depend heavily on the […] purine pathway because their salvage pathway capacity is limited, whereas most other cells recycle purines through HGPRT.
backHtml: Lymphocytes depend heavily on the de novo purine pathway because their salvage pathway capacity is limited, whereas most other cells recycle purines through HGPRT.

frontHtml: Immunosuppressive drugs: mechanisms and toxicities: Both cyclosporine and tacrolimus are narrow-therapeutic-index […].
backHtml: Both cyclosporine and tacrolimus are narrow-therapeutic-index CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein substrates.

frontHtml: Immunosuppressive drugs: mechanisms and toxicities: The blood count shows neutrophilia (demargination as endothelial and neutrophil adhesion molecules are down-regulated, plus marrow release), with […].
backHtml: The blood count shows neutrophilia (demargination as endothelial and neutrophil adhesion molecules are down-regulated, plus marrow release), with lymphopenia, eosinopenia and monocytopenia.

frontHtml: Biologics, checkpoint inhibitors and other immune drug reactions: CTLA-4 is up-regulated on activated T cells and on regulatory T cells; it binds B7 (CD80/CD86) with higher affinity than CD28 and removes B7 from antigen-presenting cells, so it acts early, in lymph nodes, to limit priming. PD-1 on chronically stimulated T cells binds […] on tumor and peripheral tissue cells and dampens T-cell receptor signaling at the effector site.
backHtml: CTLA-4 is up-regulated on activated T cells and on regulatory T cells; it binds B7 (CD80/CD86) with higher affinity than CD28 and removes B7 from antigen-presenting cells, so it acts early, in lymph nodes, to limit priming. PD-1 on chronically stimulated T cells binds PD-L1 on tumor and peripheral tissue cells and dampens T-cell receptor signaling at the effector site.

frontHtml: Biologics, checkpoint inhibitors and other immune drug reactions: Within hours of the first dose of an effective antibiotic for a spirochetal infection (syphilis, especially secondary; Lyme disease; leptospirosis; relapsing fever), lysed organisms release lipoproteins that stimulate a burst of […].
backHtml: Within hours of the first dose of an effective antibiotic for a spirochetal infection (syphilis, especially secondary; Lyme disease; leptospirosis; relapsing fever), lysed organisms release lipoproteins that stimulate a burst of TNF-α, IL-6 and IL-8.

frontHtml: Biologics, checkpoint inhibitors and other immune drug reactions: Arthus-type reactions after tetanus- or diphtheria-toxoid boosters given too frequently are […] reactions to high preformed antibody.
backHtml: Arthus-type reactions after tetanus- or diphtheria-toxoid boosters given too frequently are type III reactions to high preformed antibody.

frontHtml: HIV: diagnosis, initial evaluation and starting ART: Two to four weeks after exposure, many people develop an […]: fever, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy, a maculopapular rash on the trunk, painful mucocutaneous ulcers, myalgia, diarrhea, and sometimes aseptic meningitis.
backHtml: Two to four weeks after exposure, many people develop an acute retroviral syndrome: fever, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy, a maculopapular rash on the trunk, painful mucocutaneous ulcers, myalgia, diarrhea, and sometimes aseptic meningitis.

frontHtml: HIV: diagnosis, initial evaluation and starting ART: If the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate, run an […].
backHtml: If the differentiation assay is negative or indeterminate, run an HIV-1 RNA nucleic acid test.

frontHtml: HIV: diagnosis, initial evaluation and starting ART: ART is recommended for […], as soon as possible after diagnosis, ideally the same day or within days ( rapid start ).
backHtml: ART is recommended for everyone with HIV regardless of CD4 count, as soon as possible after diagnosis, ideally the same day or within days ( rapid start ).

frontHtml: HIV: diagnosis, initial evaluation and starting ART: Two opportunistic infections are exceptions to immediate ART because early immune recovery inflames a closed space: […] (start ART several weeks after antifungal induction, commonly 4–6 weeks) and, with specialist input, tuberculous meningitis.
backHtml: Two opportunistic infections are exceptions to immediate ART because early immune recovery inflames a closed space: cryptococcal meningitis (start ART several weeks after antifungal induction, commonly 4–6 weeks) and, with specialist input, tuberculous meningitis.

frontHtml: HIV: prevention, opportunistic-infection prophylaxis, IRIS and pregnancy: People with ongoing risk should move […] once HIV infection is excluded.
backHtml: People with ongoing risk should move directly from PEP to PrEP once HIV infection is excluded.

frontHtml: HIV: prevention, opportunistic-infection prophylaxis, IRIS and pregnancy: Management: […] and the OI treatment; give NSAIDs for mild disease and prednisone for moderate to severe paradoxical TB-IRIS.
backHtml: Management: continue ART and the OI treatment; give NSAIDs for mild disease and prednisone for moderate to severe paradoxical TB-IRIS.

frontHtml: HIV: prevention, opportunistic-infection prophylaxis, IRIS and pregnancy: Diagnose infant infection with […] (RNA or DNA), at birth for high risk and at about 14–21 days, 1–2 months and 4–6 months; maternal antibody makes antibody tests uninformative until about 18 months.
backHtml: Diagnose infant infection with HIV nucleic acid tests (RNA or DNA), at birth for high risk and at about 14–21 days, 1–2 months and 4–6 months; maternal antibody makes antibody tests uninformative until about 18 months.

frontHtml: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: recognition and management: Antihistamines and glucocorticoids […] and must never delay epinephrine.
backHtml: Antihistamines and glucocorticoids do not treat airway obstruction or shock and must never delay epinephrine.

frontHtml: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: recognition and management: Observe after resolution (longer after severe reactions or repeated epinephrine) because a […] can recur hours later without re-exposure.
backHtml: Observe after resolution (longer after severe reactions or repeated epinephrine) because a biphasic reaction can recur hours later without re-exposure.

frontHtml: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: recognition and management: Diagnosis rests on a […] (skin prick test or food-specific IgE to the suspected food).
backHtml: Diagnosis rests on a convincing history plus targeted testing (skin prick test or food-specific IgE to the suspected food).

frontHtml: Anaphylaxis and food allergy: recognition and management: The […] is the reference standard.
backHtml: The oral food challenge is the reference standard.

frontHtml: Drug hypersensitivity, contact dermatitis and tuberculin testing: The single most important step is to […].
backHtml: The single most important step is to stop every possible culprit drug immediately.

frontHtml: Drug hypersensitivity, contact dermatitis and tuberculin testing: Low-risk history (isolated GI upset, headache, family history only, or a remote benign rash without mucosal involvement, blistering or organ injury): a […] under observation, without prior skin testing.
backHtml: Low-risk history (isolated GI upset, headache, family history only, or a remote benign rash without mucosal involvement, blistering or organ injury): a direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation, without prior skin testing.

frontHtml: Drug hypersensitivity, contact dermatitis and tuberculin testing: Extensive or facial disease (for example poison ivy over more than about 20% of the body surface) warrants […]; shorter courses risk rebound.
backHtml: Extensive or facial disease (for example poison ivy over more than about 20% of the body surface) warrants oral prednisone tapered over 2–3 weeks; shorter courses risk rebound.

frontHtml: Drug hypersensitivity, contact dermatitis and tuberculin testing: An […] is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people.
backHtml: An interferon-γ release assay is preferred in BCG-vaccinated people.

frontHtml: Transplant medicine: crossmatch, rejection work-up and post-transplant infection: The […] (cPRA) estimates the percentage of donors to whom the candidate is sensitized; highly sensitized candidates (after pregnancy, transfusion or prior transplant) wait longer.
backHtml: The calculated panel-reactive antibody (cPRA) estimates the percentage of donors to whom the candidate is sensitized; highly sensitized candidates (after pregnancy, transfusion or prior transplant) wait longer.

frontHtml: Transplant medicine: crossmatch, rejection work-up and post-transplant infection: Risk is highest in a […] and after lymphocyte-depleting induction.
backHtml: Risk is highest in a seronegative recipient of a seropositive donor (D+/R−) and after lymphocyte-depleting induction.

frontHtml: Transplant medicine: crossmatch, rejection work-up and post-transplant infection: Treat with […] for severe or tissue-invasive disease, or oral valganciclovir for mild disease with reliable absorption, plus a reduction in immunosuppression; foscarnet or maribavir are used for ganciclovir-resistant virus (UL97 or UL54 mutations).
backHtml: Treat with IV ganciclovir for severe or tissue-invasive disease, or oral valganciclovir for mild disease with reliable absorption, plus a reduction in immunosuppression; foscarnet or maribavir are used for ganciclovir-resistant virus (UL97 or UL54 mutations).

frontHtml: Transplant medicine: crossmatch, rejection work-up and post-transplant infection: First-line treatment is […], then rituximab for CD20-positive disease and chemoimmunotherapy if it does not respond.
backHtml: First-line treatment is reducing immunosuppression, then rituximab for CD20-positive disease and chemoimmunotherapy if it does not respond.

frontHtml: Monitoring immunomodulating therapy: screening, immune-related adverse events and vaccine safety: Before any of these, update vaccines: […] starting, inactivated vaccines ideally at least 2 weeks before.
backHtml: Before any of these, update vaccines: live vaccines at least 4 weeks before starting, inactivated vaccines ideally at least 2 weeks before.

frontHtml: Monitoring immunomodulating therapy: screening, immune-related adverse events and vaccine safety: Low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis is taken […].
backHtml: Low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis or psoriasis is taken once weekly.

frontHtml: Monitoring immunomodulating therapy: screening, immune-related adverse events and vaccine safety: Treatment is […], which bypasses dihydrofolate reductase, plus hydration; glucarpidase is reserved for toxic levels after high-dose intravenous methotrexate with kidney failure.
backHtml: Treatment is leucovorin (folinic acid), which bypasses dihydrofolate reductase, plus hydration; glucarpidase is reserved for toxic levels after high-dose intravenous methotrexate with kidney failure.

frontHtml: Blood-borne infections: malaria, babesiosis and the intracellular pathogens: Merozoites released into the blood invade erythrocytes, where the ring, trophozoite and schizont stages cycle; synchronous schizont rupture produces the paroxysms of chills, fever and sweats, with hemolysis and splenomegaly. P. vivax and P. ovale leave dormant […] in the liver that reactivate weeks to months later, which is why radical cure needs an 8-aminoquinoline after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing.
backHtml: Merozoites released into the blood invade erythrocytes, where the ring, trophozoite and schizont stages cycle; synchronous schizont rupture produces the paroxysms of chills, fever and sweats, with hemolysis and splenomegaly. P. vivax and P. ovale leave dormant hypnozoites in the liver that reactivate weeks to months later, which is why radical cure needs an 8-aminoquinoline after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase testing.

frontHtml: Blood-borne infections: malaria, babesiosis and the intracellular pathogens: Chloroquine is a weak base concentrated in the acidic food vacuole, where it prevents polymerization of free heme into inert hemozoin; resistance follows mutations in the […] transporter.
backHtml: Chloroquine is a weak base concentrated in the acidic food vacuole, where it prevents polymerization of free heme into inert hemozoin; resistance follows mutations in the PfCRT transporter.

frontHtml: Blood-borne infections: malaria, babesiosis and the intracellular pathogens: Parvovirus B19 is a small single-stranded DNA virus that binds the […] on erythroid progenitors and lyses them, pausing erythropoiesis for one to two weeks.
backHtml: Parvovirus B19 is a small single-stranded DNA virus that binds the P antigen (globoside) on erythroid progenitors and lyses them, pausing erythropoiesis for one to two weeks.

frontHtml: Infections of lymphoid tissue: mononucleosis syndromes and infectious lymphadenitis: Epstein-Barr virus, a gamma-herpesvirus, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B lymphocytes through […], and persists for life in memory B cells.
backHtml: Epstein-Barr virus, a gamma-herpesvirus, infects oropharyngeal epithelium and then B lymphocytes through CD21, and persists for life in memory B cells.

frontHtml: Infections of lymphoid tissue: mononucleosis syndromes and infectious lymphadenitis: The atypical lymphocytes on the smear are not infected B cells but reactive […] expanding to kill them; this vigorous T-cell response causes most of the symptoms.
backHtml: The atypical lymphocytes on the smear are not infected B cells but reactive CD8+ cytotoxic T cells expanding to kill them; this vigorous T-cell response causes most of the symptoms.

frontHtml: Infections of lymphoid tissue: mononucleosis syndromes and infectious lymphadenitis: Cat-scratch disease follows inoculation of […] by a kitten scratch: an inoculation papule appears within days, and tender regional adenopathy draining that site follows one to three weeks later.
backHtml: Cat-scratch disease follows inoculation of Bartonella henselae by a kitten scratch: an inoculation papule appears within days, and tender regional adenopathy draining that site follows one to three weeks later.

frontHtml: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders of the lymphoreticular system: The clinical syndrome follows directly from these mediators: unremitting fever, hepatosplenomegaly, two- or three-lineage cytopenias, hypertriglyceridemia (TNF-alpha inhibits lipoprotein lipase), hypofibrinogenemia with coagulopathy, hepatitis, and ferritin values in the thousands. […] (soluble interleukin-2 receptor) is raised as a marker of T-cell activation, and natural killer cell function is reduced.
backHtml: The clinical syndrome follows directly from these mediators: unremitting fever, hepatosplenomegaly, two- or three-lineage cytopenias, hypertriglyceridemia (TNF-alpha inhibits lipoprotein lipase), hypofibrinogenemia with coagulopathy, hepatitis, and ferritin values in the thousands. Soluble CD25 (soluble interleukin-2 receptor) is raised as a marker of T-cell activation, and natural killer cell function is reduced.

frontHtml: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders of the lymphoreticular system: Heterozygous germline mutations in […] impair extrinsic (death receptor) apoptosis, so activated lymphocytes are not deleted after an immune response.
backHtml: Heterozygous germline mutations in FAS impair extrinsic (death receptor) apoptosis, so activated lymphocytes are not deleted after an immune response.

frontHtml: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders of the lymphoreticular system: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal neoplasm of myeloid dendritic cells with activating MAP kinase mutations, commonly […].
backHtml: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal neoplasm of myeloid dendritic cells with activating MAP kinase mutations, commonly BRAF V600E.

frontHtml: Haematologic neoplasms: lineage, genetics and morphology: Lymphoblasts express […], which adds untemplated nucleotides at antigen receptor junctions, with CD19 and CD10 and without surface immunoglobulin.
backHtml: Lymphoblasts express terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase, which adds untemplated nucleotides at antigen receptor junctions, with CD19 and CD10 and without surface immunoglobulin.

frontHtml: Haematologic neoplasms: lineage, genetics and morphology: Mantle cell lymphoma is the other CD5-positive neoplasm, but it is CD23 negative and carries […], placing CCND1 under the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer so that cyclin D1 drives the G1 to S transition.
backHtml: Mantle cell lymphoma is the other CD5-positive neoplasm, but it is CD23 negative and carries t(11;14), placing CCND1 under the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer so that cyclin D1 drives the G1 to S transition.

frontHtml: Haematologic neoplasms: lineage, genetics and morphology: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma secreting monoclonal IgM, nearly always with […]; because pentameric IgM is large and intravascular, high levels raise serum viscosity.
backHtml: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma secreting monoclonal IgM, nearly always with MYD88 L265P; because pentameric IgM is large and intravascular, high levels raise serum viscosity.

frontHtml: Blood-borne infections: diagnosis and management: Severe disease is treated with […] at any age and in pregnancy; it clears parasites faster than quinine and reduces mortality.
backHtml: Severe disease is treated with intravenous artesunate at any age and in pregnancy; it clears parasites faster than quinine and reduces mortality.

frontHtml: Blood-borne infections: diagnosis and management: Uncomplicated disease in an immunocompetent patient is treated with […], which is as effective as and better tolerated than clindamycin plus quinine.
backHtml: Uncomplicated disease in an immunocompetent patient is treated with atovaquone plus azithromycin, which is as effective as and better tolerated than clindamycin plus quinine.

frontHtml: Blood-borne infections: diagnosis and management: A sudden fall in hemoglobin with reticulocytopenia in a patient with chronic hemolysis points to […].
backHtml: A sudden fall in hemoglobin with reticulocytopenia in a patient with chronic hemolysis points to transient aplastic crisis.

frontHtml: Lymphadenopathy and lymphadenitis: evaluation and management: Cross-sectional imaging of the involved region defines the extent of disease and can disclose a mucosal or pulmonary primary tumour; it is obtained before biopsy so that sampling targets the most informative site. […] is preferred when lymphoma is suspected, because classification depends on architecture as well as immunophenotype; an adequate core needle biopsy with tissue for flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry is acceptable in many centres.
backHtml: Cross-sectional imaging of the involved region defines the extent of disease and can disclose a mucosal or pulmonary primary tumour; it is obtained before biopsy so that sampling targets the most informative site. Excisional biopsy is preferred when lymphoma is suspected, because classification depends on architecture as well as immunophenotype; an adequate core needle biopsy with tissue for flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry is acceptable in many centres.

frontHtml: Lymphadenopathy and lymphadenitis: evaluation and management: Corticosteroids are reserved for […], not for symptom relief.
backHtml: Corticosteroids are reserved for impending airway obstruction, not for symptom relief.

frontHtml: Lymphadenopathy and lymphadenitis: evaluation and management: Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis in a young child is best treated by […], with a macrolide-based regimen when excision would endanger the facial nerve; incision and drainage risks a chronic sinus.
backHtml: Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis in a young child is best treated by complete surgical excision, with a macrolide-based regimen when excision would endanger the facial nerve; incision and drainage risks a chronic sinus.

frontHtml: Hyperinflammatory and histiocytic disorders: diagnosis and management: Send ferritin early: values in the thousands, and particularly above […], are a strong pointer in adults, and extreme values are typical in children.
backHtml: Send ferritin early: values in the thousands, and particularly above 10,000 ng/mL, are a strong pointer in adults, and extreme values are typical in children.

frontHtml: Hyperinflammatory and histiocytic disorders: diagnosis and management: Idiopathic multicentric disease (HIV-negative, HHV-8-negative) is treated with the interleukin-6-directed antibody […], with corticosteroids; interleukin-6 receptor blockade and immunomodulators are alternatives.
backHtml: Idiopathic multicentric disease (HIV-negative, HHV-8-negative) is treated with the interleukin-6-directed antibody siltuximab, with corticosteroids; interleukin-6 receptor blockade and immunomodulators are alternatives.

frontHtml: Hyperinflammatory and histiocytic disorders: diagnosis and management: Multisystem disease, and any disease involving the marrow, liver or spleen, is treated with systemic chemotherapy, conventionally vinblastine with prednisone, and MAPK pathway inhibitors are used in refractory disease with BRAF V600E. […] is the commonest endocrine complication, is usually permanent, and is treated with desmopressin; growth hormone deficiency and other anterior pituitary deficits may follow.
backHtml: Multisystem disease, and any disease involving the marrow, liver or spleen, is treated with systemic chemotherapy, conventionally vinblastine with prednisone, and MAPK pathway inhibitors are used in refractory disease with BRAF V600E. Central diabetes insipidus is the commonest endocrine complication, is usually permanent, and is treated with desmopressin; growth hormone deficiency and other anterior pituitary deficits may follow.

frontHtml: Haematologic neoplasms: diagnosis, treatment and complications: In primary myelofibrosis, […] reduces spleen size and constitutional symptoms (anemia and thrombocytopenia are the main adverse effects), and transplantation is considered in higher-risk, fit patients.
backHtml: In primary myelofibrosis, ruxolitinib reduces spleen size and constitutional symptoms (anemia and thrombocytopenia are the main adverse effects), and transplantation is considered in higher-risk, fit patients.

frontHtml: Haematologic neoplasms: diagnosis, treatment and complications: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma carries a poor prognosis, and patients from endemic areas should be screened and treated for […] before immunosuppression.
backHtml: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma carries a poor prognosis, and patients from endemic areas should be screened and treated for strongyloidiasis before immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Haematologic neoplasms: diagnosis, treatment and complications: High-risk patients receive vigorous hydration plus […], which converts existing urate to allantoin within hours but is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; allopurinol suits lower-risk patients, and urinary alkalinization is no longer recommended.
backHtml: High-risk patients receive vigorous hydration plus rasburicase, which converts existing urate to allantoin within hours but is contraindicated in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; allopurinol suits lower-risk patients, and urinary alkalinization is no longer recommended.

frontHtml: Approach to anemia; iron deficiency, inflammation, lead and sideroblastic anemia: Lead inhibits […] and ferrochelatase , so aminolevulinic acid and zinc protoporphyrin accumulate.
backHtml: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase , so aminolevulinic acid and zinc protoporphyrin accumulate.

frontHtml: Approach to anemia; iron deficiency, inflammation, lead and sideroblastic anemia: It also inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA is not broken down and aggregates as […].
backHtml: It also inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA is not broken down and aggregates as coarse basophilic stippling.

frontHtml: Approach to anemia; iron deficiency, inflammation, lead and sideroblastic anemia: Iron accumulates in mitochondria around the nucleus: […] on Prussian blue stain of the marrow.
backHtml: Iron accumulates in mitochondria around the nucleus: ringed sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain of the marrow.

frontHtml: Megaloblastic anemia and marrow failure: Precursors become large with open chromatin (megaloblasts), many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis, so LDH and indirect bilirubin rise), and the blood shows oval macrocytes and […] (six or more lobes).
backHtml: Precursors become large with open chromatin (megaloblasts), many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis, so LDH and indirect bilirubin rise), and the blood shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (six or more lobes).

frontHtml: Megaloblastic anemia and marrow failure: Acid and pepsin free B 12 from food protein; it binds haptocorrin, is released by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum, binds […] from parietal cells and is taken up in the terminal ileum .
backHtml: Acid and pepsin free B 12 from food protein; it binds haptocorrin, is released by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum, binds intrinsic factor from parietal cells and is taken up in the terminal ileum .

frontHtml: Megaloblastic anemia and marrow failure: Inherited marrow failure includes […] (DNA crosslink repair defect: short stature, thumb and radial anomalies, café-au-lait spots, later leukemia and squamous cancers) and telomere disorders.
backHtml: Inherited marrow failure includes Fanconi anemia (DNA crosslink repair defect: short stature, thumb and radial anomalies, café-au-lait spots, later leukemia and squamous cancers) and telomere disorders.

frontHtml: Megaloblastic anemia and marrow failure: Erythropoietin is made by […] under the control of hypoxia-inducible factor.
backHtml: Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the renal cortex under the control of hypoxia-inducible factor.

frontHtml: Hemolysis: mechanisms, markers and the main hemolytic anemias: Proximal tubular cells reabsorb hemoglobin, store its iron as hemosiderin and shed it, so […] appears days later and persists with chronic intravascular hemolysis.
backHtml: Proximal tubular cells reabsorb hemoglobin, store its iron as hemosiderin and shed it, so urine hemosiderin appears days later and persists with chronic intravascular hemolysis.

frontHtml: Hemolysis: mechanisms, markers and the main hemolytic anemias: Some induce antibodies that react only […], often activating complement and causing brisk intravascular hemolysis (ceftriaxone and piperacillin are classic).
backHtml: Some induce antibodies that react only when the drug is present, often activating complement and causing brisk intravascular hemolysis (ceftriaxone and piperacillin are classic).

frontHtml: Hemolysis: mechanisms, markers and the main hemolytic anemias: Its progeny lack all GPI-anchored proteins, including […] (decay-accelerating factor, which limits C3 convertase) and CD59 (which blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex).
backHtml: Its progeny lack all GPI-anchored proteins, including CD55 (decay-accelerating factor, which limits C3 convertase) and CD59 (which blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex).

frontHtml: Hemolysis: mechanisms, markers and the main hemolytic anemias: Upstream intermediates accumulate, including […], which shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so patients tolerate their anemia better than expected.
backHtml: Upstream intermediates accumulate, including 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so patients tolerate their anemia better than expected.

frontHtml: Sickle cell disease, sickle trait and hemoglobin C: Hemoglobin S results from a single nucleotide change in codon 6 of the β-globin gene on chromosome 11, replacing […].
backHtml: Hemoglobin S results from a single nucleotide change in codon 6 of the β-globin gene on chromosome 11, replacing glutamate with valine.

frontHtml: Sickle cell disease, sickle trait and hemoglobin C: Hemolysis also releases free hemoglobin that scavenges […], contributing to pulmonary hypertension, priapism and leg ulcers.
backHtml: Hemolysis also releases free hemoglobin that scavenges nitric oxide, contributing to pulmonary hypertension, priapism and leg ulcers.

frontHtml: Sickle cell disease, sickle trait and hemoglobin C: Gene-based therapies either add an anti-sickling β-globin gene to autologous stem cells or edit the […] erythroid enhancer so that γ-globin (HbF) is re-expressed.
backHtml: Gene-based therapies either add an anti-sickling β-globin gene to autologous stem cells or edit the BCL11A erythroid enhancer so that γ-globin (HbF) is re-expressed.

frontHtml: Thalassemias, red cell membrane defects and porphyrias: Trait (one abnormal gene) gives marked microcytosis with a normal or high red cell count, target cells and an […].
backHtml: Trait (one abnormal gene) gives marked microcytosis with a normal or high red cell count, target cells and an HbA 2 above about 3.5%.

frontHtml: Thalassemias, red cell membrane defects and porphyrias: Unsupported lipid bilayer is lost as microvesicles, surface area falls relative to volume, and the cell becomes a dense sphere: […], spherocytes without central pallor, raised RDW.
backHtml: Unsupported lipid bilayer is lost as microvesicles, surface area falls relative to volume, and the cell becomes a dense sphere: raised MCHC, spherocytes without central pallor, raised RDW.

frontHtml: Thalassemias, red cell membrane defects and porphyrias: The rate-limiting step is […], which needs pyridoxal phosphate.
backHtml: The rate-limiting step is ALA synthase, which needs pyridoxal phosphate.

frontHtml: Thalassemias, red cell membrane defects and porphyrias: Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria: reduced hepatic […] activity, usually acquired and driven by iron in hepatocytes, with susceptibility from alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, estrogens, smoking and HFE mutations.
backHtml: Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common porphyria: reduced hepatic uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity, usually acquired and driven by iron in hepatocytes, with susceptibility from alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, estrogens, smoking and HFE mutations.

frontHtml: Iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation and anemia of CKD: evaluation and treatment: When microcytosis or a high RDW suggests iron deficiency, […] is the best single test: a ferritin below about 30 ng/mL confirms depleted stores in most adults.
backHtml: When microcytosis or a high RDW suggests iron deficiency, serum ferritin is the best single test: a ferritin below about 30 ng/mL confirms depleted stores in most adults.

frontHtml: Iron deficiency, anemia of inflammation and anemia of CKD: evaluation and treatment: Ferritin rises with inflammation, liver disease and malignancy, so in those settings add […]; a saturation below 20% with a ferritin up to about 100 ng/mL is consistent with iron deficiency alongside inflammation.
backHtml: Ferritin rises with inflammation, liver disease and malignancy, so in those settings add transferrin saturation; a saturation below 20% with a ferritin up to about 100 ng/mL is consistent with iron deficiency alongside inflammation.

frontHtml: Macrocytic anemia, aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia: diagnosis and management: When it is low-normal or symptoms are suggestive, […] (raised in B 12 but not folate deficiency) and homocysteine (raised in both) confirm tissue deficiency.
backHtml: When it is low-normal or symptoms are suggestive, methylmalonic acid (raised in B 12 but not folate deficiency) and homocysteine (raised in both) confirm tissue deficiency.

frontHtml: Macrocytic anemia, aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia: diagnosis and management: Pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count needs a […], which shows a hypocellular fatty marrow without fibrosis or abnormal cells.
backHtml: Pancytopenia with a low reticulocyte count needs a bone marrow aspirate and biopsy, which shows a hypocellular fatty marrow without fibrosis or abnormal cells.

frontHtml: Macrocytic anemia, aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia: diagnosis and management: Definitive therapy. For younger patients with severe disease and an HLA-matched sibling, […] is first-line and can cure.
backHtml: Definitive therapy. For younger patients with severe disease and an HLA-matched sibling, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is first-line and can cure.

frontHtml: Macrocytic anemia, aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia: diagnosis and management: Parvovirus B19 in an immunocompromised host (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy): […], which supplies neutralising antibody, plus reduction of immunosuppression or antiretroviral therapy where possible.
backHtml: Parvovirus B19 in an immunocompromised host (HIV, transplant, chemotherapy): intravenous immunoglobulin, which supplies neutralising antibody, plus reduction of immunosuppression or antiretroviral therapy where possible.

frontHtml: Hemolytic anemia: workup and management: Sutimlimab, a monoclonal antibody to […], blocks the classical complement pathway and reduces hemolysis.
backHtml: Sutimlimab, a monoclonal antibody to C1s, blocks the classical complement pathway and reduces hemolysis.

frontHtml: Hemolytic anemia: workup and management: Complement inhibition for symptomatic hemolysis or thrombosis: the […] eculizumab and ravulizumab stop intravascular hemolysis and greatly reduce thrombosis.
backHtml: Complement inhibition for symptomatic hemolysis or thrombosis: the C5 inhibitors eculizumab and ravulizumab stop intravascular hemolysis and greatly reduce thrombosis.

frontHtml: Hemolytic anemia: workup and management: Confirm the diagnosis with a quantitative G6PD assay about 3 months after the episode, because […] falsely raise activity. Test G6PD before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine (radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale ), rasburicase, or dapsone where possible.
backHtml: Confirm the diagnosis with a quantitative G6PD assay about 3 months after the episode, because reticulocytes falsely raise activity. Test G6PD before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine (radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale ), rasburicase, or dapsone where possible.

frontHtml: Sickle cell disease: health maintenance and acute complications: Stroke screening: annual […] ultrasonography from age 2 to 16 years in HbSS and HbS-β 0 -thalassemia.
backHtml: Stroke screening: annual transcranial Doppler ultrasonography from age 2 to 16 years in HbSS and HbS-β 0 -thalassemia.

frontHtml: Sickle cell disease: health maintenance and acute complications: A time-averaged mean maximum velocity of 200 cm/s or more (confirmed) is abnormal and calls for a […] aiming to keep HbS below about 30%, which reduces first stroke dramatically.
backHtml: A time-averaged mean maximum velocity of 200 cm/s or more (confirmed) is abnormal and calls for a chronic transfusion program aiming to keep HbS below about 30%, which reduces first stroke dramatically.

frontHtml: Sickle cell disease: health maintenance and acute complications: Do a history and examination, CBC with reticulocyte count and blood culture, then give a […], without waiting for results.
backHtml: Do a history and examination, CBC with reticulocyte count and blood culture, then give a parenteral third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) promptly, without waiting for results.

frontHtml: Thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis and porphyrias: management: Check […], because iron deficiency lowers HbA 2 and can mask β-thalassemia trait.
backHtml: Check ferritin first, because iron deficiency lowers HbA 2 and can mask β-thalassemia trait.

frontHtml: Thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis and porphyrias: management: Diagnose with a family history, spherocytes, a raised MCHC, a negative DAT and a reduced […] test.
backHtml: Diagnose with a family history, spherocytes, a raised MCHC, a negative DAT and a reduced EMA binding test.

frontHtml: Thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis and porphyrias: management: The best initial test is a […] (normalised to creatinine) during the attack; a marked rise confirms an acute hepatic porphyria.
backHtml: The best initial test is a spot urine porphobilinogen (normalised to creatinine) during the attack; a marked rise confirms an acute hepatic porphyria.

frontHtml: Thalassemia, hereditary spherocytosis and porphyrias: management: Treatment is […] to lower hepatic iron (target ferritin near the low end of normal) or low-dose hydroxychloroquine (standard doses can cause hepatotoxicity in PCT), plus sun protection and removal of triggers.
backHtml: Treatment is therapeutic phlebotomy to lower hepatic iron (target ferritin near the low end of normal) or low-dose hydroxychloroquine (standard doses can cause hepatotoxicity in PCT), plus sun protection and removal of triggers.

frontHtml: Acute blood loss and anemia of systemic disease: The hemoglobin falls over the next hours and reaches its true new level only after […] of equilibration.
backHtml: The hemoglobin falls over the next hours and reaches its true new level only after about 24 to 72 hours of equilibration.

frontHtml: Acute blood loss and anemia of systemic disease: In the meantime a […] are common.
backHtml: In the meantime a neutrophilic leukocytosis and reactive thrombocytosis are common.

frontHtml: Acute blood loss and anemia of systemic disease: The red cells in liver disease are often mildly […] (round macrocytes from excess membrane lipid), so the neutrophils are not hypersegmented unless folate deficiency is also present.
backHtml: The red cells in liver disease are often mildly macrocytic without megaloblastic change (round macrocytes from excess membrane lipid), so the neutrophils are not hypersegmented unless folate deficiency is also present.

frontHtml: Physiologic, dilutional and life-stage anemias: Together these produce the […]: in term infants hemoglobin falls to roughly 9 to 11 g/dL at about 2 to 3 months, after which erythropoietin rises and production resumes.
backHtml: Together these produce the physiologic nadir: in term infants hemoglobin falls to roughly 9 to 11 g/dL at about 2 to 3 months, after which erythropoietin rises and production resumes.

frontHtml: Physiologic, dilutional and life-stage anemias: In […] the fall comes earlier and goes deeper.
backHtml: In preterm infants the fall comes earlier and goes deeper.

frontHtml: Physiologic, dilutional and life-stage anemias: The clue is a […] and a dimorphic smear with both small hypochromic cells and large oval macrocytes, sometimes with hypersegmented neutrophils.
backHtml: The clue is a high RDW and a dimorphic smear with both small hypochromic cells and large oval macrocytes, sometimes with hypersegmented neutrophils.

frontHtml: Physiologic, dilutional and life-stage anemias: Anemia is common in older adults but is […].
backHtml: Anemia is common in older adults but is not a normal consequence of ageing.

frontHtml: Neutropenia, agranulocytosis and lymphopenia: The […] is the total leukocyte count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands.
backHtml: The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) is the total leukocyte count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands.

frontHtml: Neutropenia, agranulocytosis and lymphopenia: Cyclic neutropenia. Autosomal dominant variants in ELANE (neutrophil elastase) cause regular cycles, usually about […], of severe neutropenia lasting several days with fever, mouth ulcers and gingivitis.
backHtml: Cyclic neutropenia. Autosomal dominant variants in ELANE (neutrophil elastase) cause regular cycles, usually about every 21 days, of severe neutropenia lasting several days with fever, mouth ulcers and gingivitis.

frontHtml: Neutropenia, agranulocytosis and lymphopenia: Gram-negative rods including […] are the classic early killers, so empiric therapy is an intravenous anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam started promptly after cultures.
backHtml: Gram-negative rods including Pseudomonas aeruginosa are the classic early killers, so empiric therapy is an intravenous anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam started promptly after cultures.

frontHtml: Thrombocytopenia: mechanisms, ITP and the differential: The patient has no bleeding, the smear shows clumps, and a count in a […] (or heparin) tube is normal.
backHtml: The patient has no bleeding, the smear shows clumps, and a count in a citrate (or heparin) tube is normal.

frontHtml: Thrombocytopenia: mechanisms, ITP and the differential: IgG autoantibodies, most often against […] or Ib/IX, coat platelets, which are then removed by splenic macrophages through Fc-gamma receptors.
backHtml: IgG autoantibodies, most often against glycoprotein IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX, coat platelets, which are then removed by splenic macrophages through Fc-gamma receptors.

frontHtml: Thrombocytopenia: mechanisms, ITP and the differential: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: IgG against […] activates platelets through Fc-gamma RIIa; the count falls 5 to 10 days after heparin starts and the risk is thrombosis, not bleeding.
backHtml: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: IgG against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes activates platelets through Fc-gamma RIIa; the count falls 5 to 10 days after heparin starts and the risk is thrombosis, not bleeding.

frontHtml: Polycythemia vera and secondary erythrocytosis: In […] the red cell mass is normal and the plasma volume is reduced: dehydration, diuretics, burns, or the chronic low plasma volume seen in some people with obesity, hypertension and smoking.
backHtml: In relative (apparent) polycythemia the red cell mass is normal and the plasma volume is reduced: dehydration, diuretics, burns, or the chronic low plasma volume seen in some people with obesity, hypertension and smoking.

frontHtml: Polycythemia vera and secondary erythrocytosis: In […] red cell mass is truly increased, either from a clonal marrow disorder (polycythemia vera) or from an erythropoietin-driven process (secondary erythrocytosis).
backHtml: In absolute erythrocytosis red cell mass is truly increased, either from a clonal marrow disorder (polycythemia vera) or from an erythropoietin-driven process (secondary erythrocytosis).

frontHtml: Polycythemia vera and secondary erythrocytosis: About 95% of patients carry the […] mutation, and most of the rest have a JAK2 exon 12 mutation.
backHtml: About 95% of patients carry the JAK2 V617F mutation, and most of the rest have a JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and eosinophilia: ET is a diagnosis of exclusion: reactive causes and other myeloid neoplasms must be ruled out, especially […] (test for BCR-ABL1), which can present with a high platelet count alone.
backHtml: ET is a diagnosis of exclusion: reactive causes and other myeloid neoplasms must be ruled out, especially CML (test for BCR-ABL1), which can present with a high platelet count alone.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and eosinophilia: At platelet counts above about 1,000,000/mm 3 , large von Willebrand multimers adsorb to the platelet surface and are cleared, producing an […] and a bleeding tendency.
backHtml: At platelet counts above about 1,000,000/mm 3 , large von Willebrand multimers adsorb to the platelet surface and are cleared, producing an acquired von Willebrand syndrome and a bleeding tendency.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and eosinophilia: A […] is an extreme reactive leukocytosis, typically above 50,000/mm 3 , with a left shift to bands, metamyelocytes and a few myelocytes.
backHtml: A leukemoid reaction is an extreme reactive leukocytosis, typically above 50,000/mm 3 , with a left shift to bands, metamyelocytes and a few myelocytes.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis and eosinophilia: In […] (sustained hypereosinophilia with organ damage), the heart is the most feared target: endomyocardial necrosis, mural thrombus and then fibrosis cause a restrictive cardiomyopathy.
backHtml: In hypereosinophilic syndrome (sustained hypereosinophilia with organ damage), the heart is the most feared target: endomyocardial necrosis, mural thrombus and then fibrosis cause a restrictive cardiomyopathy.

frontHtml: Acute blood loss, transfusion thresholds and anemia in liver disease: In acute hemorrhage the decision to transfuse is driven by […], not by the first hemoglobin, which lags behind the true deficit until plasma volume is restored over the next one to three days.
backHtml: In acute hemorrhage the decision to transfuse is driven by hemodynamics and ongoing loss, not by the first hemoglobin, which lags behind the true deficit until plasma volume is restored over the next one to three days.

frontHtml: Acute blood loss, transfusion thresholds and anemia in liver disease: Patients in hemorrhagic shock receive blood products early, in a […] (approximately 1:1:1) through a massive transfusion protocol, with tranexamic acid in trauma when it can be given within 3 hours of injury.
backHtml: Patients in hemorrhagic shock receive blood products early, in a balanced ratio of plasma, platelets and red cells (approximately 1:1:1) through a massive transfusion protocol, with tranexamic acid in trauma when it can be given within 3 hours of injury.

frontHtml: Acute blood loss, transfusion thresholds and anemia in liver disease: Work up anemia in cirrhosis systematically: look for […] (varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, peptic ulcer), iron deficiency , folate deficiency (poor diet in alcohol use disorder), hypersplenism, hemolysis, and medication effects (for example ribavirin in older hepatitis C regimens).
backHtml: Work up anemia in cirrhosis systematically: look for gastrointestinal blood loss (varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy, peptic ulcer), iron deficiency , folate deficiency (poor diet in alcohol use disorder), hypersplenism, hemolysis, and medication effects (for example ribavirin in older hepatitis C regimens).

frontHtml: Anemia in pregnancy, infancy, toddlers, athletes and older adults: Check ferritin; a ferritin below about […] confirms deficiency in pregnancy.
backHtml: Check ferritin; a ferritin below about 30 ng/mL confirms deficiency in pregnancy.

frontHtml: Anemia in pregnancy, infancy, toddlers, athletes and older adults: A rise of […] confirms iron deficiency; continue iron for about 3 months after the count normalises to replete stores.
backHtml: A rise of at least 1 g/dL confirms iron deficiency; continue iron for about 3 months after the count normalises to replete stores.

frontHtml: Anemia in pregnancy, infancy, toddlers, athletes and older adults: An endurance athlete with a slightly low hemoglobin, normal MCV, normal ferritin and no symptoms most likely has […] from plasma volume expansion; no treatment is needed.
backHtml: An endurance athlete with a slightly low hemoglobin, normal MCV, normal ferritin and no symptoms most likely has dilutional pseudoanemia from plasma volume expansion; no treatment is needed.

frontHtml: Neutropenia, pancytopenia and lymphopenia: evaluation and management: Agranulocytosis with one thionamide is a contraindication to the other because of […]; definitive therapy (radioactive iodine or surgery) is then chosen.
backHtml: Agranulocytosis with one thionamide is a contraindication to the other because of cross-reactivity; definitive therapy (radioactive iodine or surgery) is then chosen.

frontHtml: Neutropenia, pancytopenia and lymphopenia: evaluation and management: Fever persisting for 4 to 7 days despite antibiotics prompts a search and empiric therapy for […].
backHtml: Fever persisting for 4 to 7 days despite antibiotics prompts a search and empiric therapy for invasive fungal infection.

frontHtml: Neutropenia, pancytopenia and lymphopenia: evaluation and management: The […] is the most informative test when the cause is not apparent, and it is urgent if blasts are seen.
backHtml: The bone marrow aspirate and biopsy is the most informative test when the cause is not apparent, and it is urgent if blasts are seen.

frontHtml: Thrombocytopenia: approach, ITP management and special populations: In adults, testing for […] is recommended because treating them can improve the count, and many clinicians test for H. pylori and check thyroid function, immunoglobulins and a direct antiglobulin test.
backHtml: In adults, testing for HIV and hepatitis C is recommended because treating them can improve the count, and many clinicians test for H. pylori and check thyroid function, immunoglobulins and a direct antiglobulin test.

frontHtml: Thrombocytopenia: approach, ITP management and special populations: NAIT presents as petechiae, bruising or, most seriously, intracranial hemorrhage (sometimes in utero) in an otherwise well newborn whose […].
backHtml: NAIT presents as petechiae, bruising or, most seriously, intracranial hemorrhage (sometimes in utero) in an otherwise well newborn whose mother has a normal platelet count.

frontHtml: Erythrocytosis and polycythemia vera: work-up and management: If JAK2 V617F is negative but erythropoietin is low, test for a […] mutation.
backHtml: If JAK2 V617F is negative but erythropoietin is low, test for a JAK2 exon 12 mutation.

frontHtml: Erythrocytosis and polycythemia vera: work-up and management: The resulting iron deficiency is intended; […] unless symptomatic iron deficiency demands it, because it will drive red cell production.
backHtml: The resulting iron deficiency is intended; do not give iron unless symptomatic iron deficiency demands it, because it will drive red cell production.

frontHtml: Erythrocytosis and polycythemia vera: work-up and management: Cytoreduction is added for high-risk patients, defined by […] or a previous thrombosis, and for others with poor tolerance of phlebotomy, progressive splenomegaly, symptomatic thrombocytosis or leukocytosis, or severe symptoms.
backHtml: Cytoreduction is added for high-risk patients, defined by age 60 or older or a previous thrombosis, and for others with poor tolerance of phlebotomy, progressive splenomegaly, symptomatic thrombocytosis or leukocytosis, or severe symptoms.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, eosinophilia and neonatal polycythemia: management: The first steps are to repeat the count, review the smear and look for a cause: […], recent surgery or trauma, infection, inflammatory disease, malignancy and splenectomy.
backHtml: The first steps are to repeat the count, review the smear and look for a cause: ferritin and iron studies, CRP, recent surgery or trauma, infection, inflammatory disease, malignancy and splenectomy.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, eosinophilia and neonatal polycythemia: management: If the count stays above 450,000/mm 3 without a cause, test for […], and refer for marrow examination.
backHtml: If the count stays above 450,000/mm 3 without a cause, test for JAK2 V617F, CALR and MPL mutations and BCR-ABL1, and refer for marrow examination.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, eosinophilia and neonatal polycythemia: management: A capillary (heel-stick) hematocrit runs higher than venous blood, so […] before acting.
backHtml: A capillary (heel-stick) hematocrit runs higher than venous blood, so confirm with a venous sample before acting.

frontHtml: Thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, eosinophilia and neonatal polycythemia: management: Symptomatic hyperviscosity (lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, seizures), especially at higher hematocrits: […], replacing blood with normal saline to lower the hematocrit; evidence of long-term benefit is limited, so it is reserved for symptomatic infants.
backHtml: Symptomatic hyperviscosity (lethargy, poor feeding, respiratory distress, seizures), especially at higher hematocrits: partial exchange transfusion, replacing blood with normal saline to lower the hematocrit; evidence of long-term benefit is limited, so it is reserved for symptomatic infants.

frontHtml: Hemostasis and the screening coagulation tests: At a site of injury, von Willebrand factor (vWF) unfolds on exposed subendothelial collagen and binds platelet […] (adhesion).
backHtml: At a site of injury, von Willebrand factor (vWF) unfolds on exposed subendothelial collagen and binds platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V (adhesion).

frontHtml: Hemostasis and the screening coagulation tests: Activation switches […] (integrin αIIbβ3) into a high-affinity state, so fibrinogen can bridge neighbouring platelets (aggregation). Secondary hemostasis is the coagulation cascade, which generates thrombin and turns the loose plug into a cross-linked fibrin clot.
backHtml: Activation switches GpIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) into a high-affinity state, so fibrinogen can bridge neighbouring platelets (aggregation). Secondary hemostasis is the coagulation cascade, which generates thrombin and turns the loose plug into a cross-linked fibrin clot.

frontHtml: Hemostasis and the screening coagulation tests: An isolated prolonged aPTT is first repeated to exclude heparin contamination (samples drawn from a heparinized line), then tested with a […].
backHtml: An isolated prolonged aPTT is first repeated to exclude heparin contamination (samples drawn from a heparinized line), then tested with a 1:1 mixing study.

frontHtml: Inherited and acquired factor disorders: About a third of cases arise from new mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude it; an inversion within […] of F8 causes almost half of severe hemophilia A.
backHtml: About a third of cases arise from new mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude it; an inversion within intron 22 of F8 causes almost half of severe hemophilia A.

frontHtml: Inherited and acquired factor disorders: PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and platelets are all normal; the clot dissolves in […], and a factor XIII activity assay confirms.
backHtml: PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and platelets are all normal; the clot dissolves in 5 M urea, and a factor XIII activity assay confirms.

frontHtml: Inherited and acquired factor disorders: Vitamin K is the cofactor for […], which adds a carboxyl group to glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.
backHtml: Vitamin K is the cofactor for γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds a carboxyl group to glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S.

frontHtml: Platelet function disorders and consumptive coagulopathy: Repeated transfusion can induce antibodies against the missing glycoprotein, making later transfusions ineffective; […] is an alternative in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
backHtml: Repeated transfusion can induce antibodies against the missing glycoprotein, making later transfusions ineffective; recombinant factor VIIa is an alternative in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

frontHtml: Platelet function disorders and consumptive coagulopathy: Dialysis, correcting anemia (red cells push platelets toward the vessel wall), desmopressin for rapid effect and […] for longer effect all help.
backHtml: Dialysis, correcting anemia (red cells push platelets toward the vessel wall), desmopressin for rapid effect and conjugated estrogens for longer effect all help.

frontHtml: Platelet function disorders and consumptive coagulopathy: Fibrinogen is an […], so a "normal" level in a septic patient may already be falling; serial values matter more than a single one.
backHtml: Fibrinogen is an acute phase protein, so a "normal" level in a septic patient may already be falling; serial values matter more than a single one.

frontHtml: Thrombophilia and the mechanisms of anticoagulant drugs: Thrombosis needs one or more of: stasis (immobility, long travel, heart failure, venous compression by a gravid uterus), […] (surgery, trauma, catheters, vasculitis, smoking for arterial disease) and hypercoagulability (inherited or acquired).
backHtml: Thrombosis needs one or more of: stasis (immobility, long travel, heart failure, venous compression by a gravid uterus), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma, catheters, vasculitis, smoking for arterial disease) and hypercoagulability (inherited or acquired).

frontHtml: Thrombophilia and the mechanisms of anticoagulant drugs: Activated protein C, with its cofactor […], cleaves and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.
backHtml: Activated protein C, with its cofactor protein S, cleaves and inactivates factors Va and VIIIa.

frontHtml: Mechanisms of transfusion reactions: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is almost always […] caused by a clerical or identification error.
backHtml: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is almost always ABO incompatibility caused by a clerical or identification error.

frontHtml: Mechanisms of transfusion reactions: IgG-coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis): falling hemoglobin, mild jaundice, spherocytes, a positive DAT with IgG and a newly identified alloantibody. […] antibodies are known for fading quickly and then returning strongly.
backHtml: IgG-coated cells are removed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis): falling hemoglobin, mild jaundice, spherocytes, a positive DAT with IgG and a newly identified alloantibody. Kidd antibodies are known for fading quickly and then returning strongly.

frontHtml: Mechanisms of transfusion reactions: Refrigerated red cells favour cold-growing, iron-loving organisms such as […].
backHtml: Refrigerated red cells favour cold-growing, iron-loving organisms such as Yersinia enterocolitica.

frontHtml: Evaluating bleeding and managing inherited bleeding disorders: Watch for […] (fluid restriction) and tachyphylaxis after several doses; avoid in young children at seizure risk.
backHtml: Watch for hyponatremia (fluid restriction) and tachyphylaxis after several doses; avoid in young children at seizure risk.

frontHtml: Evaluating bleeding and managing inherited bleeding disorders: Low-titer inhibitors (under […]) can sometimes be overwhelmed with higher factor doses; high-titer inhibitors need bypassing agents (recombinant factor VIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate).
backHtml: Low-titer inhibitors (under 5 Bethesda units) can sometimes be overwhelmed with higher factor doses; high-titer inhibitors need bypassing agents (recombinant factor VIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate).

frontHtml: Evaluating bleeding and managing inherited bleeding disorders: Hemostasis uses bypassing agents (recombinant VIIa or activated PCC) or […]; human factor VIII and desmopressin are usually ineffective against a strong inhibitor.
backHtml: Hemostasis uses bypassing agents (recombinant VIIa or activated PCC) or recombinant porcine factor VIII; human factor VIII and desmopressin are usually ineffective against a strong inhibitor.

frontHtml: Acquired coagulopathies: vitamin K, liver disease, DIC and uremia: Newborn prophylaxis. Every newborn should receive a […] of vitamin K (phytonadione) soon after birth.
backHtml: Newborn prophylaxis. Every newborn should receive a single intramuscular dose of vitamin K (phytonadione) soon after birth.

frontHtml: Acquired coagulopathies: vitamin K, liver disease, DIC and uremia: The only definitive treatment is removing the trigger: antibiotics and source control in sepsis, delivery of the fetus and placenta in obstetric DIC, […] in acute promyelocytic leukemia.
