backHtml: The only definitive treatment is removing the trigger: antibiotics and source control in sepsis, delivery of the fetus and placenta in obstetric DIC, all-trans retinoic acid in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

frontHtml: Acquired coagulopathies: vitamin K, liver disease, DIC and uremia: For active bleeding or before an urgent procedure (kidney biopsy, line placement), give […], which acts within about an hour and lasts several hours; repeated doses lose effect. Conjugated estrogens act over days and last about 2 weeks, which suits recurrent bleeding (for example from angiodysplasia). Dialysis and correcting anemia (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, transfusion toward a hematocrit around 30%) improve platelet function.
backHtml: For active bleeding or before an urgent procedure (kidney biopsy, line placement), give desmopressin, which acts within about an hour and lasts several hours; repeated doses lose effect. Conjugated estrogens act over days and last about 2 weeks, which suits recurrent bleeding (for example from angiodysplasia). Dialysis and correcting anemia (erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, transfusion toward a hematocrit around 30%) improve platelet function.

frontHtml: Diagnosing deep vein thrombosis: Diagnosis starts by estimating pretest probability, most often with the […].
backHtml: Diagnosis starts by estimating pretest probability, most often with the Wells score for DVT.

frontHtml: Diagnosing deep vein thrombosis: […] is the first-line imaging test: a vein that does not collapse under probe pressure contains thrombus.
backHtml: Compression ultrasonography is the first-line imaging test: a vein that does not collapse under probe pressure contains thrombus.

frontHtml: Diagnosing deep vein thrombosis: For suspected PE, an age-adjusted cutoff ([…] in patients over 50) increases specificity in older adults without losing safety.
backHtml: For suspected PE, an age-adjusted cutoff (age × 10 µg/L FEU in patients over 50) increases specificity in older adults without losing safety.

frontHtml: Treating VTE: drug choice, duration and thrombophilia testing: An […] is indicated only for acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (for example, active bleeding); retrieve it and start anticoagulation once safe.
backHtml: An IVC filter is indicated only for acute proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation is contraindicated (for example, active bleeding); retrieve it and start anticoagulation once safe.

frontHtml: Treating VTE: drug choice, duration and thrombophilia testing: Suspected […] (unprovoked VTE in a young patient, arterial thrombosis at a young age, thrombosis at an unusual site, recurrent pregnancy loss, unexplained prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia with thrombosis): a positive result changes drug choice (warfarin rather than a DOAC).
backHtml: Suspected antiphospholipid syndrome (unprovoked VTE in a young patient, arterial thrombosis at a young age, thrombosis at an unusual site, recurrent pregnancy loss, unexplained prolonged aPTT, thrombocytopenia with thrombosis): a positive result changes drug choice (warfarin rather than a DOAC).

frontHtml: Blood products: indications and managing transfusion reactions: A restrictive strategy is standard for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults: transfuse at a hemoglobin below […] (including most ICU patients and those with GI bleeding).
backHtml: A restrictive strategy is standard for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults: transfuse at a hemoglobin below 7 g/dL (including most ICU patients and those with GI bleeding).

frontHtml: Blood products: indications and managing transfusion reactions: Give […] in stable patients and reassess; one unit raises hemoglobin by about 1 g/dL in an average adult.
backHtml: Give one unit at a time in stable patients and reassess; one unit raises hemoglobin by about 1 g/dL in an average adult.

frontHtml: Blood products: indications and managing transfusion reactions: For any reaction other than isolated mild hives: […], keep the IV line open with normal saline, check vital signs, recheck the patient's identity against the unit label, and notify the blood bank.
backHtml: For any reaction other than isolated mild hives: stop the transfusion, keep the IV line open with normal saline, check vital signs, recheck the patient's identity against the unit label, and notify the blood bank.

frontHtml: Massive transfusion and hemostatic resuscitation: Because these definitions are retrospective, hospitals use a […] activated on clinical grounds.
backHtml: Because these definitions are retrospective, hospitals use a massive transfusion protocol activated on clinical grounds.

frontHtml: Massive transfusion and hemostatic resuscitation: Balanced ratio : give plasma, platelets and red cells in a ratio close to […] (whole blood, where available, provides the same).
backHtml: Balanced ratio : give plasma, platelets and red cells in a ratio close to 1:1:1 (whole blood, where available, provides the same).

frontHtml: Mechanical and microangiopathic red-cell destruction: Two broad settings produce it: […] (abnormal heart valves, ventricular assist devices, repetitive external impact) and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) , in which cells are sliced by fibrin or platelet thrombi in small vessels.
backHtml: Two broad settings produce it: macrovascular shear (abnormal heart valves, ventricular assist devices, repetitive external impact) and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA) , in which cells are sliced by fibrin or platelet thrombi in small vessels.

frontHtml: Mechanical and microangiopathic red-cell destruction: Raised […] and unconjugated bilirubin; reticulocytosis if the marrow is healthy.
backHtml: Raised LDH and unconjugated bilirubin; reticulocytosis if the marrow is healthy.

frontHtml: Splenic structure, filtering and immune function: The spleen develops from […] (mesoderm), yet it is supplied by the splenic artery , a branch of the celiac trunk (the foregut artery).
backHtml: The spleen develops from mesenchyme in the dorsal mesogastrium (mesoderm), yet it is supplied by the splenic artery , a branch of the celiac trunk (the foregut artery).

frontHtml: Splenic structure, filtering and immune function: The […] carries the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.
backHtml: The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.

frontHtml: Splenic structure, filtering and immune function: Surrounding both is the […], where blood slows and is sampled by specialized macrophages and marginal-zone B cells .
backHtml: Surrounding both is the marginal zone, where blood slows and is sampled by specialized macrophages and marginal-zone B cells .

frontHtml: Splenic structure, filtering and immune function: Functional : […], where repeated sickling and infarction cause functional asplenia in infancy and a small fibrotic spleen (autosplenectomy) by later childhood; celiac disease ; alcohol-related liver disease; systemic lupus erythematosus; amyloidosis; graft-versus-host disease; splenic irradiation.
backHtml: Functional : sickle cell anemia, where repeated sickling and infarction cause functional asplenia in infancy and a small fibrotic spleen (autosplenectomy) by later childhood; celiac disease ; alcohol-related liver disease; systemic lupus erythematosus; amyloidosis; graft-versus-host disease; splenic irradiation.

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, hypersplenism, rupture and infarction: mechanisms: Massive splenomegaly (crossing the midline or reaching the pelvis) narrows the list to myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, myelofibrosis), hairy cell leukemia, some lymphomas, Gaucher disease, thalassemia major, chronic malaria and […].
backHtml: Massive splenomegaly (crossing the midline or reaching the pelvis) narrows the list to myeloproliferative neoplasms (CML, myelofibrosis), hairy cell leukemia, some lymphomas, Gaucher disease, thalassemia major, chronic malaria and visceral leishmaniasis.

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, hypersplenism, rupture and infarction: mechanisms: The spleen has an end-arterial supply, so occlusion of a segmental branch produces a wedge-shaped, pale (anemic) infarct with […], its base at the capsule.
backHtml: The spleen has an end-arterial supply, so occlusion of a segmental branch produces a wedge-shaped, pale (anemic) infarct with coagulative necrosis, its base at the capsule.

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, hypersplenism, rupture and infarction: mechanisms: Before autosplenectomy, a sudden pooling of blood in the spleen causes […]: rapid enlargement of the spleen, an acute fall in hemoglobin with a maintained or raised reticulocyte count, often thrombocytopenia, and risk of hypovolemic shock.
backHtml: Before autosplenectomy, a sudden pooling of blood in the spleen causes acute splenic sequestration: rapid enlargement of the spleen, an acute fall in hemoglobin with a maintained or raised reticulocyte count, often thrombocytopenia, and risk of hypovolemic shock.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic drugs: mechanisms, toxicity and reversal: Warfarin inhibits […], so reduced vitamin K is not regenerated and the hepatic gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S fails.
backHtml: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so reduced vitamin K is not regenerated and the hepatic gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S fails.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic drugs: mechanisms, toxicity and reversal: Reversal uses vitamin K (slow, needs new factor synthesis) and, for serious bleeding, […], which supplies II, VII, IX and X immediately.
backHtml: Reversal uses vitamin K (slow, needs new factor synthesis) and, for serious bleeding, 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC), which supplies II, VII, IX and X immediately.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic drugs: mechanisms, toxicity and reversal: Reversal options are […], a recombinant, catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds the drug, or 4-factor PCC.
backHtml: Reversal options are andexanet alfa, a recombinant, catalytically inactive factor Xa decoy that binds the drug, or 4-factor PCC.

frontHtml: Drug-induced cytopenias, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia and tumor lysis: Non-chemotherapy causes include […], clozapine, sulfasalazine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, dapsone, deferiprone and procainamide.
backHtml: Non-chemotherapy causes include methimazole and propylthiouracil, clozapine, sulfasalazine, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, dapsone, deferiprone and procainamide.

frontHtml: Drug-induced cytopenias, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia and tumor lysis: Oxidant drugs convert heme iron from ferrous (Fe 2+ ) to […].
backHtml: Oxidant drugs convert heme iron from ferrous (Fe 2+ ) to ferric (Fe 3+ ).

frontHtml: Drug-induced cytopenias, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia and tumor lysis: Purines are degraded to […], which crystallizes in acidic renal tubules; calcium phosphate precipitates as well, and secondary hypocalcemia follows.
backHtml: Purines are degraded to uric acid, which crystallizes in acidic renal tubules; calcium phosphate precipitates as well, and secondary hypocalcemia follows.

frontHtml: Drug-induced cytopenias, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia and tumor lysis: The reaction produces […], which in G6PD deficiency causes severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.
backHtml: The reaction produces hydrogen peroxide, which in G6PD deficiency causes severe hemolysis and methemoglobinemia.

frontHtml: Thrombotic microangiopathy and mechanical hemolysis: diagnosis and management: When a patient has anemia with schistocytes, the first job is to decide whether the problem is a […], which can kill within days, or mechanical damage from a valve, device or external trauma, which is rarely urgent.
backHtml: When a patient has anemia with schistocytes, the first job is to decide whether the problem is a thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), which can kill within days, or mechanical damage from a valve, device or external trauma, which is rarely urgent.

frontHtml: Thrombotic microangiopathy and mechanical hemolysis: diagnosis and management: Draw […] (and inhibitor) before plasma is given, but never wait for the result to treat.
backHtml: Draw ADAMTS13 activity (and inhibitor) before plasma is given, but never wait for the result to treat.

frontHtml: Thrombotic microangiopathy and mechanical hemolysis: diagnosis and management: Plasma exchange may be started while ADAMTS13 is pending; once TTP and STEC are excluded, a […] (eculizumab or ravulizumab) is first-line.
backHtml: Plasma exchange may be started while ADAMTS13 is pending; once TTP and STEC are excluded, a C5 inhibitor (eculizumab or ravulizumab) is first-line.

frontHtml: Thrombotic microangiopathy and mechanical hemolysis: diagnosis and management: Transthoracic echocardiography comes first, but acoustic shadowing from the prosthesis often hides mitral paravalvular jets, so […] is the most accurate test.
backHtml: Transthoracic echocardiography comes first, but acoustic shadowing from the prosthesis often hides mitral paravalvular jets, so transesophageal echocardiography is the most accurate test.

frontHtml: Caring for the asplenic patient: vaccines, prophylaxis and fever: Every patient without a functioning spleen carries a lifelong risk of […]: fulminant bacteremia, usually pneumococcal, that can progress from a flu-like illness to septic shock, DIC and purpura fulminans within hours.
backHtml: Every patient without a functioning spleen carries a lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI): fulminant bacteremia, usually pneumococcal, that can progress from a flu-like illness to septic shock, DIC and purpura fulminans within hours.

frontHtml: Caring for the asplenic patient: vaccines, prophylaxis and fever: Timing around splenectomy. For an elective splenectomy, give vaccines […], so that antibody responses form while the spleen is present.
backHtml: Timing around splenectomy. For an elective splenectomy, give vaccines at least 2 weeks before surgery, so that antibody responses form while the spleen is present.

frontHtml: Caring for the asplenic patient: vaccines, prophylaxis and fever: Every asplenic patient should carry a […] (for example amoxicillin-clavulanate, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone or cefuroxime with penicillin allergy), start it at the first sign of fever if care is not immediately available, and then seek urgent assessment.
backHtml: Every asplenic patient should carry a standby antibiotic (for example amoxicillin-clavulanate, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone or cefuroxime with penicillin allergy), start it at the first sign of fever if care is not immediately available, and then seek urgent assessment.

frontHtml: Caring for the asplenic patient: vaccines, prophylaxis and fever: Obtain blood cultures and give […] immediately, without waiting for laboratory results or imaging.
backHtml: Obtain blood cultures and give empiric IV ceftriaxone immediately, without waiting for laboratory results or imaging.

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, splenic trauma, infarction and sequestration: management: Hemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation with intraperitoneal fluid on FAST: […] (splenectomy or splenorrhaphy).
backHtml: Hemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation with intraperitoneal fluid on FAST: exploratory laparotomy (splenectomy or splenorrhaphy).

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, splenic trauma, infarction and sequestration: management: A […] (endocarditis, injection drug use, immunosuppression) causes fever, left upper quadrant pain and sometimes a left pleural effusion; treatment is antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage, with splenectomy for multiloculated or refractory cases.
backHtml: A splenic abscess (endocarditis, injection drug use, immunosuppression) causes fever, left upper quadrant pain and sometimes a left pleural effusion; treatment is antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage, with splenectomy for multiloculated or refractory cases.

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, splenic trauma, infarction and sequestration: management: Restore circulating volume and give […] promptly, in modest volumes, because the spleen releases trapped cells as it shrinks and over-transfusion can cause hyperviscosity.
backHtml: Restore circulating volume and give red-cell transfusion promptly, in modest volumes, because the spleen releases trapped cells as it shrinks and over-transfusion can cause hyperviscosity.

frontHtml: Splenomegaly, splenic trauma, infarction and sequestration: management: If ITP relapses after splenectomy and the smear shows […], suspect an accessory spleen; scintigraphy with heat-damaged radiolabelled red cells localizes it, and laparoscopic removal can restore remission.
backHtml: If ITP relapses after splenectomy and the smear shows no Howell-Jolly bodies, suspect an accessory spleen; scintigraphy with heat-damaged radiolabelled red cells localizes it, and laparoscopic removal can restore remission.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic bleeding: reversal and safe prescribing: Warfarin, not a DOAC, is the oral anticoagulant for […] and for high-risk (triple-positive) antiphospholipid syndrome.
backHtml: Warfarin, not a DOAC, is the oral anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves and for high-risk (triple-positive) antiphospholipid syndrome.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic bleeding: reversal and safe prescribing: Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban : […] or 4-factor PCC , according to local availability and protocols.
backHtml: Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban : andexanet alfa or 4-factor PCC , according to local availability and protocols.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic bleeding: reversal and safe prescribing: Unfractionated heparin has a short half-life; for serious bleeding give […], dosed on the heparin given in the previous few hours.
backHtml: Unfractionated heparin has a short half-life; for serious bleeding give protamine sulfate, dosed on the heparin given in the previous few hours.

frontHtml: Chemotherapy and drug toxicity to blood: recognition and management: The […] equals the white-cell count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands.
backHtml: The absolute neutrophil count (ANC) equals the white-cell count multiplied by the fraction of segmented neutrophils plus bands.

frontHtml: Chemotherapy and drug toxicity to blood: recognition and management: Febrile neutropenia : blood cultures (peripheral and from any line) and an empiric […] (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) within an hour.
backHtml: Febrile neutropenia : blood cultures (peripheral and from any line) and an empiric antipseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) within an hour.

frontHtml: Chemotherapy and drug toxicity to blood: recognition and management: In […], methylene blue is avoided; options are ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen.
backHtml: In G6PD deficiency, methylene blue is avoided; options are ascorbic acid, exchange transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen.

frontHtml: Chemotherapy and drug toxicity to blood: recognition and management: Rasburicase for high risk or established hyperuricemia; screen patients at risk for […] first, and use allopurinol instead if deficient.
backHtml: Rasburicase for high risk or established hyperuricemia; screen patients at risk for G6PD deficiency first, and use allopurinol instead if deficient.

frontHtml: Newborn physiology, growth and infant nutrition: With the first breaths, alveolar expansion and the rise in alveolar oxygen dilate pulmonary arterioles, so […] steeply.
backHtml: With the first breaths, alveolar expansion and the rise in alveolar oxygen dilate pulmonary arterioles, so pulmonary vascular resistance falls steeply.

frontHtml: Newborn physiology, growth and infant nutrition: The […] constricts because two signals change together: arterial PO 2 rises, and circulating prostaglandin E 2 falls (the placenta that made it is gone and the now-perfused lungs metabolise it).
backHtml: The ductus arteriosus constricts because two signals change together: arterial PO 2 rises, and circulating prostaglandin E 2 falls (the placenta that made it is gone and the now-perfused lungs metabolise it).

frontHtml: Newborn physiology, growth and infant nutrition: less bilirubin conjugated: hepatic […] activity is low at birth and matures over the first weeks;
backHtml: less bilirubin conjugated: hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) activity is low at birth and matures over the first weeks;

frontHtml: Newborn physiology, growth and infant nutrition: Breast milk adds […], made by mammary plasma cells primed in the maternal gut, which coats the infant's intestinal mucosa without being absorbed.
backHtml: Breast milk adds secretory IgA, made by mammary plasma cells primed in the maternal gut, which coats the infant's intestinal mucosa without being absorbed.

frontHtml: Developmental milestones, primitive reflexes and normal variants: Development is assessed in four streams: […], fine motor/visual-motor , language and social-emotional .
backHtml: Development is assessed in four streams: gross motor, fine motor/visual-motor , language and social-emotional .

frontHtml: Developmental milestones, primitive reflexes and normal variants: For infants born preterm, use […] until about 2 years.
backHtml: For infants born preterm, use corrected age until about 2 years.

frontHtml: Developmental milestones, primitive reflexes and normal variants: A clear […] suggests weakness of the other arm (for example hemiplegic cerebral palsy or brachial plexus injury).
backHtml: A clear hand preference before about 12–18 months suggests weakness of the other arm (for example hemiplegic cerebral palsy or brachial plexus injury).

frontHtml: Physiology of puberty and adolescent development: The first hormonal sign is a […]; daytime pulses follow later.
backHtml: The first hormonal sign is a sleep-associated rise in LH pulse amplitude; daytime pulses follow later.

frontHtml: Physiology of puberty and adolescent development: Boys : […] is the first sign, at about 11–12 years (range roughly 9–14); most of testicular volume is seminiferous tubules, so the growth reflects FSH-driven Sertoli and germ cell expansion.
backHtml: Boys : testicular enlargement is the first sign, at about 11–12 years (range roughly 9–14); most of testicular volume is seminiferous tubules, so the growth reflects FSH-driven Sertoli and germ cell expansion.

frontHtml: Newborn screening and childhood surveillance: The […] is collected at about 24–48 hours of age.
backHtml: The dried blood-spot screen is collected at about 24–48 hours of age.

frontHtml: Newborn screening and childhood surveillance: A positive screen is […]: it triggers confirmatory testing, with urgency matched to the disorder.
backHtml: A positive screen is not a diagnosis: it triggers confirmatory testing, with urgency matched to the disorder.

frontHtml: Newborn screening and childhood surveillance: An infant who does not pass the screen and the rescreen needs a […] (including diagnostic ABR) before 3 months; waiting for speech delay forfeits the critical period for language.
backHtml: An infant who does not pass the screen and the rescreen needs a diagnostic audiologic evaluation (including diagnostic ABR) before 3 months; waiting for speech delay forfeits the critical period for language.

frontHtml: Newborn screening and childhood surveillance: Formal […] is done at 9, 18 and 30 months, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months, or whenever a parent or clinician is concerned.
backHtml: Formal standardised developmental screening is done at 9, 18 and 30 months, and autism-specific screening at 18 and 24 months, or whenever a parent or clinician is concerned.

frontHtml: Immunization principles, anticipatory guidance and growth faltering: Practical rules: inactivated vaccines can be given together or at any interval; two […] (MMR, varicella) are given on the same day or at least 28 days apart.
backHtml: Practical rules: inactivated vaccines can be given together or at any interval; two live parenteral vaccines (MMR, varicella) are given on the same day or at least 28 days apart.

frontHtml: Immunization principles, anticipatory guidance and growth faltering: BMI is plotted from age 2. Obesity is a BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex; […] is at or above 120% of the 95th percentile.
backHtml: BMI is plotted from age 2. Obesity is a BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex; severe obesity is at or above 120% of the 95th percentile.

frontHtml: Immunization principles, anticipatory guidance and growth faltering: The […] narrows the cause.
backHtml: The pattern of the curves narrows the cause.

frontHtml: Immunization principles, anticipatory guidance and growth faltering: The most useful evaluation is a […] (what, how much, how prepared, who feeds), a psychosocial history, a careful examination and, where possible, observation of a feed.
backHtml: The most useful evaluation is a detailed feeding and dietary history (what, how much, how prepared, who feeds), a psychosocial history, a careful examination and, where possible, observation of a feed.

frontHtml: The adolescent preventive visit: For chlamydia and gonorrhea, a […] (self-collected is acceptable) is the preferred specimen in females; urine NAAT is acceptable.
backHtml: For chlamydia and gonorrhea, a vaginal swab NAAT (self-collected is acceptable) is the preferred specimen in females; urine NAAT is acceptable.

frontHtml: The adolescent preventive visit: Cervical cancer screening does not start before […], whatever the age of sexual debut, and a pelvic examination is not required to screen for STIs or to start contraception.
backHtml: Cervical cancer screening does not start before age 21, whatever the age of sexual debut, and a pelvic examination is not required to screen for STIs or to start contraception.

frontHtml: The adolescent preventive visit: Depot medroxyprogesterone lowers […] while used, which is reversible and not a reason to deny it.
backHtml: Depot medroxyprogesterone lowers bone mineral density while used, which is reversible and not a reason to deny it.

frontHtml: Disorders of pubertal timing and the pre-participation evaluation: Puberty is precocious when secondary sexual characteristics begin before […] or 9 years in boys .
backHtml: Puberty is precocious when secondary sexual characteristics begin before 8 years in girls or 9 years in boys .

frontHtml: Disorders of pubertal timing and the pre-participation evaluation: Once central precocious puberty is confirmed, […] is obtained in all boys, and in girls with neurological signs or very early onset (younger ages carry a higher chance of a lesion).
backHtml: Once central precocious puberty is confirmed, brain MRI is obtained in all boys, and in girls with neurological signs or very early onset (younger ages carry a higher chance of a lesion).

frontHtml: Disorders of pubertal timing and the pre-participation evaluation: Its main safety goal is to identify adolescents at risk of […] during exertion, most often from inherited cardiomyopathies (such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), anomalous coronary arteries, channelopathies (long QT syndrome) and aortic disease (Marfan syndrome).
backHtml: Its main safety goal is to identify adolescents at risk of sudden cardiac death during exertion, most often from inherited cardiomyopathies (such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), anomalous coronary arteries, channelopathies (long QT syndrome) and aortic disease (Marfan syndrome).

frontHtml: Disorders of pubertal timing and the pre-participation evaluation: A positive history or examination means […] (ECG and echocardiography, with cardiology referral).
backHtml: A positive history or examination means no clearance until cardiac evaluation (ECG and echocardiography, with cardiology referral).

frontHtml: Physiology across adulthood: bone, fitness, sleep, sexual response and grief: The largest single contributor is the fall in […], which reflects reduced sinoatrial responsiveness to catecholamines rather than any change in resting heart rate.
backHtml: The largest single contributor is the fall in maximal heart rate, which reflects reduced sinoatrial responsiveness to catecholamines rather than any change in resting heart rate.

frontHtml: Physiology across adulthood: bone, fitness, sleep, sexual response and grief: Shift work misaligns the circadian clock, which is entrained mainly by light acting on the […].
backHtml: Shift work misaligns the circadian clock, which is entrained mainly by light acting on the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

frontHtml: Physiology across adulthood: bone, fitness, sleep, sexual response and grief: Self-worth is preserved, and function gradually returns. Prolonged grief disorder is diagnosed in adults when intense yearning or preoccupation persists, most days, […] after the loss and impairs function.
backHtml: Self-worth is preserved, and function gradually returns. Prolonged grief disorder is diagnosed in adults when intense yearning or preoccupation persists, most days, at least 12 months after the loss and impairs function.

frontHtml: Perimenopause, menopause and the aging male axis: Menopause is defined retrospectively as […] after the final menstrual period; the median age in the United States is about 51.
backHtml: Menopause is defined retrospectively as 12 months without menses after the final menstrual period; the median age in the United States is about 51.

frontHtml: Perimenopause, menopause and the aging male axis: Their […] output, acting on neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptors in the preoptic thermoregulatory area, narrows the thermoneutral zone, so a small rise in core temperature triggers peripheral vasodilation, flushing and sweating.
backHtml: Their neurokinin B output, acting on neurokinin 3 (NK3) receptors in the preoptic thermoregulatory area, narrows the thermoneutral zone, so a small rise in core temperature triggers peripheral vasodilation, flushing and sweating.

frontHtml: Perimenopause, menopause and the aging male axis: Estrogen deficiency therefore causes […]: resorption outpaces formation, and trabecular bone is lost fastest.
backHtml: Estrogen deficiency therefore causes high-turnover bone loss: resorption outpaces formation, and trabecular bone is lost fastest.

frontHtml: Perimenopause, menopause and the aging male axis: Total testosterone falls gradually from middle age, and sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) rises, so […].
backHtml: Total testosterone falls gradually from middle age, and sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) rises, so free testosterone falls more than total.

frontHtml: Physiology of aging by organ system: The left ventricle thickens and relaxes more slowly, so early diastolic filling falls and the […] becomes important; an S4 can be heard and loss of atrial kick in atrial fibrillation is poorly tolerated.
backHtml: The left ventricle thickens and relaxes more slowly, so early diastolic filling falls and the atrial contribution becomes important; an S4 can be heard and loss of atrial kick in atrial fibrillation is poorly tolerated.

frontHtml: Physiology of aging by organ system: Airways close earlier in expiration, so […] while vital capacity falls; total lung capacity is about unchanged.
backHtml: Airways close earlier in expiration, so residual volume and functional residual capacity rise while vital capacity falls; total lung capacity is about unchanged.

frontHtml: Physiology of aging by organ system: Nephron number and renal blood flow fall, and […] on average from middle age.
backHtml: Nephron number and renal blood flow fall, and GFR declines on average from middle age.

frontHtml: Physiology of aging by organ system: Combined with a […] to hyperosmolality and lower total body water, this predisposes to hypernatremia during illness or heat; impaired free-water excretion predisposes to hyponatremia with thiazides or SSRIs.
backHtml: Combined with a reduced thirst response to hyperosmolality and lower total body water, this predisposes to hypernatremia during illness or heat; impaired free-water excretion predisposes to hyponatremia with thiazides or SSRIs.

frontHtml: Drug handling in older adults and normal cognitive aging: Water-soluble drugs (lithium, digoxin, ethanol, aminoglycosides) distribute into a smaller volume, so the same dose gives a […].
backHtml: Water-soluble drugs (lithium, digoxin, ethanol, aminoglycosides) distribute into a smaller volume, so the same dose gives a higher plasma concentration.

frontHtml: Drug handling in older adults and normal cognitive aging: Because half-life is proportional to volume of distribution divided by clearance (t ½ = 0.693 × V d /CL), a […] and the drug accumulates with repeated doses.
backHtml: Because half-life is proportional to volume of distribution divided by clearance (t ½ = 0.693 × V d /CL), a larger V d prolongs half-life and the drug accumulates with repeated doses.

frontHtml: Drug handling in older adults and normal cognitive aging: Smaller liver mass and reduced hepatic blood flow lower […] (oxidation, reduction, hydroxylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes) capacity. Phase II conjugation, especially glucuronidation, is relatively preserved.
backHtml: Smaller liver mass and reduced hepatic blood flow lower phase I (oxidation, reduction, hydroxylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes) capacity. Phase II conjugation, especially glucuronidation, is relatively preserved.

frontHtml: Drug handling in older adults and normal cognitive aging: Older adults are more sensitive to the central effects of benzodiazepines, opioids, sedative hypnotics and anticholinergic drugs because neuronal and especially […] is reduced.
backHtml: Older adults are more sensitive to the central effects of benzodiazepines, opioids, sedative hypnotics and anticholinergic drugs because neuronal and especially cholinergic reserve is reduced.

frontHtml: Adult screening from 18 to 64: Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) grades: […] means offer the service, C means offer selectively after individual discussion, D means do not offer, and I means the evidence is insufficient.
backHtml: Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) grades: A or B means offer the service, C means offer selectively after individual discussion, D means do not offer, and I means the evidence is insufficient.

frontHtml: Adult screening from 18 to 64: Offer a statin when risk is […]; at 7.5% to under 10%, offer selectively after discussion.
backHtml: Offer a statin when risk is 10% or higher; at 7.5% to under 10%, offer selectively after discussion.

frontHtml: Adult screening from 18 to 64: Chlamydia and gonorrhea : sexually active women 24 and younger, and older women at increased risk. Syphilis and […]: adults at increased risk.
backHtml: Chlamydia and gonorrhea : sexually active women 24 and younger, and older women at increased risk. Syphilis and latent tuberculosis: adults at increased risk.

frontHtml: Adult screening from 18 to 64: Screen women of reproductive age for […] and connect those who disclose it with ongoing support services.
backHtml: Screen women of reproductive age for intimate partner violence and connect those who disclose it with ongoing support services.

frontHtml: Counselling, chemoprevention and immunizations in adults: Unhealthy use without features of alcohol use disorder calls for […] (feedback, advice, goal setting, follow-up).
backHtml: Unhealthy use without features of alcohol use disorder calls for brief counselling (feedback, advice, goal setting, follow-up).

frontHtml: Counselling, chemoprevention and immunizations in adults: Adults with a […] should be offered or referred to an intensive, multicomponent behavioral intervention (many sessions over a year covering diet, activity, self-monitoring and problem solving).
backHtml: Adults with a BMI of 30 or more should be offered or referred to an intensive, multicomponent behavioral intervention (many sessions over a year covering diet, activity, self-monitoring and problem solving).

frontHtml: Counselling, chemoprevention and immunizations in adults: After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, a higher dose of […] is recommended before and in early pregnancy.
backHtml: After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, a higher dose of 4 mg daily is recommended before and in early pregnancy.

frontHtml: Comprehensive geriatric assessment, falls and medication safety: A positive answer, or a fall with injury, leads to a […]:
backHtml: A positive answer, or a fall with injury, leads to a multifactorial assessment:

frontHtml: Comprehensive geriatric assessment, falls and medication safety: Gait, strength and balance : a Timed Up and Go of […] suggests increased risk; chair-stand and balance tests add detail.
backHtml: Gait, strength and balance : a Timed Up and Go of 12 seconds or longer suggests increased risk; chair-stand and balance tests add detail.

frontHtml: Comprehensive geriatric assessment, falls and medication safety: Polypharmacy (commonly defined as […]) raises the risk of adverse drug events, interactions, nonadherence, falls and hospitalization.
backHtml: Polypharmacy (commonly defined as five or more regular medicines) raises the risk of adverse drug events, interactions, nonadherence, falls and hospitalization.

frontHtml: Screening, immunization and stopping rules after 65: Screen […] with bone mineral density testing by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip and lumbar spine.
backHtml: Screen all women 65 and older with bone mineral density testing by dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) of the hip and lumbar spine.

frontHtml: Screening, immunization and stopping rules after 65: Men […] (100 or more cigarettes in a lifetime) should have a one-time abdominal ultrasound .
backHtml: Men 65–75 who have ever smoked (100 or more cigarettes in a lifetime) should have a one-time abdominal ultrasound .

frontHtml: Screening, immunization and stopping rules after 65: Pneumococcal : if no prior conjugate vaccine, one dose of […] completes the series; alternatively PCV15 followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later.
backHtml: Pneumococcal : if no prior conjugate vaccine, one dose of PCV20 or PCV21 completes the series; alternatively PCV15 followed by PPSV23 at least 1 year later.

frontHtml: Screening, immunization and stopping rules after 65: RSV : a […] for all adults 75 and older, and for adults 60–74 at increased risk (chronic heart or lung disease, diabetes with complications, chronic kidney disease, immunocompromise, nursing-home residence, frailty).
backHtml: RSV : a single dose for all adults 75 and older, and for adults 60–74 at increased risk (chronic heart or lung disease, diabetes with complications, chronic kidney disease, immunocompromise, nursing-home residence, frailty).

frontHtml: Continence, frailty, nutrition, driving and advance care planning: Interventions are […], adequate protein and energy intake, deprescribing, and treatment of contributing illness.
backHtml: Interventions are progressive resistance and balance exercise, adequate protein and energy intake, deprescribing, and treatment of contributing illness.

frontHtml: Continence, frailty, nutrition, driving and advance care planning: Management treats the cause, […] (low-salt, diabetic or low-cholesterol diets add little in frail adults and reduce intake), adds oral nutritional supplements, assistance at meals and meal delivery.
backHtml: Management treats the cause, liberalizes restrictive diets (low-salt, diabetic or low-cholesterol diets add little in frail adults and reduce intake), adds oral nutritional supplements, assistance at meals and meal delivery.

frontHtml: Continence, frailty, nutrition, driving and advance care planning: A […] (living will) describing treatments wanted or refused in defined situations.
backHtml: A written advance directive (living will) describing treatments wanted or refused in defined situations.

frontHtml: Continence, frailty, nutrition, driving and advance care planning: For seriously ill or frail people, […] (such as a POLST form) that translate preferences into actionable orders across settings.
backHtml: For seriously ill or frail people, portable medical orders (such as a POLST form) that translate preferences into actionable orders across settings.

frontHtml: Explain why absent B cells predispose to chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis.
backHtml: chronic enteroviral meningoencephalitis is a signature infection of B-cell absence because enterovirus clearance depends on neutralizing antibody.

frontHtml: Identify the cellular defect in common variable immunodeficiency from immunoglobulin, vaccine and B-cell findings.
backHtml: CVID has B cells but not enough plasma cells; X-linked agammaglobulinemia lacks the B cells themselves.

frontHtml: Describe how secretory IgM, transported by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor, compensates for selective IgA deficiency.
backHtml: J-chain–containing IgM uses the same pIgR transport route as IgA, which helps compensate mucosal defence in IgA deficiency.

frontHtml: Relate activation-induced cytidine deaminase deficiency to hyper-IgM with lymphoid hyperplasia.
backHtml: AID deficiency is the B-intrinsic hyper-IgM: large germinal centres, pyogenic infections only, normal CD40L.

frontHtml: Identify the cell type that expresses CD40 ligand and link its loss to opportunistic infection in X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome.
backHtml: CD40L is a T-cell molecule, so its loss impairs both B-cell switching and macrophage activation.

frontHtml: Explain the physiological basis of transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy.
backHtml: low IgG with normal B cells and normal vaccine responses in an infant that later normalises is delayed maturation, not a fixed defect.

frontHtml: Distinguish T-independent polysaccharide responses from T-dependent conjugate responses in specific antibody deficiency.
backHtml: specific antibody deficiency is a failure of T-independent polysaccharide responses; conjugate vaccines work because they make the response T-dependent.

frontHtml: Link loss of IL-7 signalling through the common γ chain to T-cell absence in X-linked SCID.
backHtml: in γc deficiency, absent IL-7 signalling removes T cells and absent IL-15 signalling removes NK cells.

frontHtml: Explain how adenosine deaminase deficiency causes lymphocyte death through dATP accumulation.
backHtml: ADA-SCID is a purine metabolic disease in which dATP is toxic to lymphocytes.

frontHtml: Recognize Omenn syndrome as leaky SCID from hypomorphic defects in V(D)J recombination.
backHtml: Omenn syndrome is leaky SCID: residual V(D)J recombination yields a few autoreactive T-cell clones and no B cells.

frontHtml: Locate the lymph node compartment depleted in T-cell aplasia.
backHtml: T-cell deficiency empties the paracortex; B-cell deficiency empties follicles and germinal centres.

frontHtml: Identify the actin-regulating function of WAS protein from the Wiskott-Aldrich triad.
backHtml: WAS protein is a hematopoietic actin regulator; its loss gives small platelets, eczema and poor polysaccharide antibody responses.

frontHtml: Relate ATM deficiency to hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation in ataxia-telangiectasia.
backHtml: ATM loss means radiosensitivity; minimise diagnostic radiation in ataxia-telangiectasia.

frontHtml: Use serum IFN-γ level to localize a defect in the IL-12/IFN-γ axis.
backHtml: in mycobacterial susceptibility, raised IFN-γ localises the defect to the IFN-γ receptor.

frontHtml: Link STAT3 dominant-negative hyper-IgE syndrome to failed Th17 differentiation.
backHtml: STAT3 hyper-IgE is a Th17 failure; the barrier, not the bloodstream, is undefended.

frontHtml: Explain why early classical complement deficiency predisposes to systemic lupus erythematosus.
backHtml: early classical complement deficiency causes lupus because apoptotic debris and immune complexes are not cleared.

frontHtml: Classify hereditary angioedema from C4, C1q and C1 inhibitor level and function.
backHtml: HAE type I has low C1-INH level and function; type II has normal level and low function; both have low C4 and normal C1q.

frontHtml: Identify properdin deficiency from X-linked inheritance and a low AH50 with normal CH50.
backHtml: normal CH50 with low AH50 means factor B, factor D or properdin; X-linked meningococcal disease points to properdin.

frontHtml: Explain how factor H dysfunction causes atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.
backHtml: atypical HUS is complement-mediated endothelial injury from failed surface regulation of the alternative pathway; C5 blockade is the treatment.

frontHtml: Relate C3 deficiency to failed opsonization of encapsulated bacteria.
backHtml: C3 is the hub of complement; its loss removes C3b opsonization and causes severe pyogenic infection.

frontHtml: Identify the infectious risk of C5 inhibition by eculizumab.
backHtml: anti-C5 therapy means meningococcal risk; vaccinate and educate.

frontHtml: Localize a complement deficiency using CH50, AH50 and individual component levels.
backHtml: low CH50 with normal AH50, normal C4 and normal C1q points to C2 deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the classic catalase hypothesis for the organisms that infect patients with chronic granulomatous disease.
backHtml: CGD infections are classically catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Burkholderia, Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus).

frontHtml: Identify leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 2 as a fucosylation defect affecting selectin ligands.
backHtml: LAD-2 is a fucosylation defect: no selectin-mediated rolling and Bombay phenotype.

frontHtml: Identify myeloperoxidase deficiency and the reaction it impairs.
backHtml: MPO deficiency: normal NBT, absent peroxidase staining, invasive Candida mostly in diabetes.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of ELANE-related severe congenital neutropenia.
backHtml: ELANE-related congenital neutropenia is an intrinsic marrow defect: misfolded elastase kills precursors.

frontHtml: Explain how failed lymphocyte cytotoxicity drives familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
backHtml: familial HLH is failed cytotoxicity: the stimulus is never removed, so activation never stops.

frontHtml: Choose quantitative immunoglobulins as the first immunologic test for recurrent sinopulmonary infection.
backHtml: recurrent sinopulmonary infection: quantitative immunoglobulins first, then vaccine responses.

frontHtml: Order specific antibody testing before immunoglobulin replacement in suspected CVID.
backHtml: test vaccine responses before starting IgG replacement for moderate hypogammaglobulinemia.

frontHtml: Switch to subcutaneous immunoglobulin after recurrent systemic reactions to IVIG.
backHtml: systemic IVIG reactions that persist despite rate changes and premedication are an indication to switch to SCIG.

frontHtml: Choose IgG-based celiac serology in a patient with selective IgA deficiency.
backHtml: in IgA deficiency, test for celiac disease with IgG-based serology.

frontHtml: Select washed or IgA-deficient blood products for a patient with prior anti-IgA transfusion anaphylaxis.
backHtml: anti-IgA anaphylaxis history: washed cellular products or IgA-deficient donor blood.

frontHtml: Manage transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy with observation and repeat testing.
backHtml: low IgG with normal vaccine responses in an infant warrants follow-up testing, not replacement.

frontHtml: Diagnose specific antibody deficiency from a poor polysaccharide response with normal immunoglobulin levels.
backHtml: recurrent pneumonia with normal immunoglobulins does not exclude antibody deficiency: test polysaccharide responses.

frontHtml: Order lymphocyte flow cytometry after an abnormal TREC newborn screen.
backHtml: abnormal TREC newborn screen: flow cytometry next, without delay.

frontHtml: Choose appropriate protective measures for an infant with SCID awaiting transplantation.
backHtml: before transplant in SCID: Pneumocystis prophylaxis, IgG, no live vaccines, irradiated CMV-safe blood.

frontHtml: Recommend hematopoietic stem cell transplantation as definitive therapy for SCID.
backHtml: SCID is a paediatric emergency treated definitively by early HSCT.

frontHtml: Order irradiated blood products for an infant with 22q11.2 deletion before T-cell status is known.
backHtml: suspected or possible T-cell deficiency: irradiate all cellular blood products.

frontHtml: Recommend hematopoietic stem cell transplantation for classic Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
backHtml: classic WAS is treated definitively with early HSCT.

frontHtml: Order serum α-fetoprotein to support suspected ataxia-telangiectasia.
backHtml: toddler-onset ataxia with sinopulmonary infections: check AFP for ataxia-telangiectasia.

frontHtml: Screen for adrenal insufficiency in a patient with APECED.
backHtml: candidiasis plus hypoparathyroidism means APECED: screen for adrenal insufficiency.

frontHtml: Prescribe anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis in STAT3 hyper-IgE syndrome.
backHtml: STAT3 hyper-IgE: daily anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis and barrier care.

frontHtml: Treat an acute laryngeal attack of hereditary angioedema with C1 inhibitor concentrate.
backHtml: HAE laryngeal attack: secure the airway and give C1-INH concentrate, icatibant or ecallantide.

frontHtml: Select plasma-derived C1 inhibitor for preprocedural prophylaxis in a pregnant patient with hereditary angioedema.
backHtml: preprocedural HAE prophylaxis is plasma-derived C1-INH, which is also the agent of choice in pregnancy.

frontHtml: Manage ACE-inhibitor angioedema by stopping the ACE inhibitor and choosing another antihypertensive class.
backHtml: ACE-inhibitor angioedema: stop the class for good; avoid neprilysin inhibitors; switch to another drug class.

frontHtml: Evaluate for a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder in acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency.
backHtml: late-onset angioedema with low C1q: look for a B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder.

frontHtml: Plan meningococcal vaccination before starting a C5 inhibitor.
backHtml: before C5 inhibition: MenACWY plus MenB, at least 2 weeks ahead, and teach the patient to seek care for fever.

frontHtml: Prevent recurrent meningococcal disease in terminal complement deficiency with meningococcal vaccination.
backHtml: terminal complement deficiency: vaccinate against all meningococcal serogroups, keep boosting, and screen siblings.

frontHtml: Screen with CH50 for early classical complement deficiency in childhood lupus with recurrent bacteremia.
backHtml: childhood lupus with recurrent encapsulated-bacterial infection: screen complement with CH50.

frontHtml: Prescribe trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and itraconazole prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease.
backHtml: CGD prophylaxis is TMP-SMX plus a mold-active azole (itraconazole), with optional IFN-γ.

frontHtml: Identify live bacterial vaccines as contraindicated in chronic granulomatous disease.
backHtml: CGD: no live bacterial vaccines; live viral and inactivated vaccines are fine.

frontHtml: Document cyclic neutropenia with serial CBCs over 6 weeks.
backHtml: periodic fever with mouth ulcers: serial neutrophil counts to look for cyclic neutropenia.

frontHtml: Treat severe congenital neutropenia with G-CSF and arrange marrow surveillance.
backHtml: severe congenital neutropenia: G-CSF plus marrow surveillance for MDS/AML.

frontHtml: Begin HLH-94–based induction therapy for familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
backHtml: familial HLH: induce remission with dexamethasone and etoposide (plus intrathecal therapy for CNS disease), then transplant.

frontHtml: Confirm leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 with CD18 flow cytometry.
backHtml: neutrophilia without pus and delayed cord separation: test CD18 by flow cytometry.

frontHtml: Recognize myelodysplasia and leukemia risk in GATA2 deficiency.
backHtml: GATA2 deficiency: mycobacteria, warts, absent monocytes and NK cells, and a high risk of MDS/AML.

frontHtml: Explain how CCR5-Δ32 homozygosity protects against R5-tropic HIV-1 entry.
backHtml: CCR5-Δ32 homozygosity blocks the coreceptor step of HIV entry and protects against R5-tropic virus.

frontHtml: Identify NNRTIs as inactive against HIV-2 and explain why.
backHtml: HIV-2 is intrinsically resistant to NNRTIs; build regimens from NRTIs plus an INSTI or a boosted protease inhibitor.

frontHtml: Identify the latent proviral reservoir in resting memory CD4+ T cells as the source of viral rebound after stopping ART.
backHtml: The latent reservoir of integrated provirus in resting memory CD4+ T cells is why ART controls but does not cure HIV.

frontHtml: Recognize tenofovir disoproxil fumarate-induced Fanconi syndrome as proximal tubular injury.
backHtml: Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate causes proximal tubulopathy (Fanconi syndrome) and bone loss.

frontHtml: Link the histology of Kaposi sarcoma to human herpesvirus 8.
backHtml: Kaposi sarcoma is an HHV-8-driven spindle-cell vascular tumor that appears at low CD4 counts.

frontHtml: Recognize HIV-associated nephropathy and its collapsing FSGS histology.
backHtml: HIVAN is collapsing FSGS presenting with heavy proteinuria and large echogenic kidneys; treat with ART and RAAS blockade.

frontHtml: Identify cross-linking of FcεRI-bound IgE as the trigger of a type I hypersensitivity reaction.
backHtml: Type I reactions start when allergen cross-links FcεRI-bound IgE on a previously sensitized mast cell.

frontHtml: Recognize pemphigus vulgaris as a type II hypersensitivity against desmosomal proteins.
backHtml: Antibody against a fixed cell-surface or matrix antigen (here desmoglein) is type II hypersensitivity.

frontHtml: Explain the Arthus reaction as localized immune-complex (type III) vasculitis.
backHtml: An Arthus reaction is a local type III reaction: immune complexes plus complement and neutrophils in vessel walls, peaking within hours.

frontHtml: Identify allergic contact dermatitis as a T-cell–mediated type IV reaction to a hapten.
backHtml: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed (type IV) T-cell reaction to a hapten, appearing 1–3 days after re-exposure.

frontHtml: Recognize alpha-gal syndrome as delayed IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to a mammalian carbohydrate after tick bites.
backHtml: Delayed anaphylaxis hours after red meat, after tick bites, points to IgE against the carbohydrate alpha-gal.

frontHtml: Explain the IL-5–driven eosinophilic late-phase response of type I hypersensitivity.
backHtml: The late-phase allergic response is an eosinophil-rich, Th2 (IL-5)-driven infiltrate that follows mast cell degranulation by hours.

frontHtml: Identify acute T cell–mediated rejection and its mechanism on a kidney-transplant biopsy.
backHtml: Tubulitis without C4d weeks after a kidney transplant is acute T cell–mediated rejection against donor MHC.

frontHtml: Recognize peritubular C4d as the marker of antibody-mediated transplant rejection.
backHtml: Donor-specific antibodies plus capillaritis and peritubular C4d indicate antibody-mediated rejection.

frontHtml: Recognize bronchiolitis obliterans as chronic rejection after lung transplantation.
backHtml: Progressive obstruction with fibrous obliteration of bronchioles years after lung transplant is chronic rejection.

frontHtml: Explain acute GVHD as donor T cells attacking recipient skin, gut and liver.
backHtml: Rash, diarrhea and cholestasis around engraftment after allogeneic stem cell transplant are acute graft-versus-host disease.

frontHtml: Calculate the probability that a full sibling is HLA-identical from haplotype inheritance.
backHtml: Each full sibling has a 25% chance of being HLA-identical, 50% haploidentical and 25% fully mismatched.

frontHtml: Explain post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder as EBV-driven B-cell growth released from T-cell surveillance.
backHtml: PTLD is EBV-driven B-cell proliferation that escapes T-cell control under transplant immunosuppression; reduce immunosuppression first.

frontHtml: Rank CMV risk by donor and recipient serostatus after solid-organ transplantation.
backHtml: CMV risk after solid-organ transplant is highest in a seronegative recipient of a seropositive organ (D+/R−).

frontHtml: Explain the azathioprine–xanthine oxidase inhibitor interaction that causes marrow suppression.
backHtml: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol, febuxostat) raise thiopurine levels and can cause pancytopenia with azathioprine.

frontHtml: Relate inherited TPMT deficiency to thiopurine-induced myelosuppression.
backHtml: Check TPMT (and NUDT15) before thiopurines; deficiency causes severe myelosuppression at normal doses.

frontHtml: Explain how tacrolimus prevents IL-2 transcription through calcineurin–NFAT inhibition.
backHtml: Calcineurin inhibitors block NFAT dephosphorylation and therefore IL-2 transcription, downstream of the calcium signal.

frontHtml: Identify mTOR inhibition by sirolimus and its characteristic adverse effects.
backHtml: Sirolimus inhibits mTORC1; it spares the kidney but causes hyperlipidemia and poor wound healing.

frontHtml: Explain why IMP dehydrogenase inhibition selectively suppresses lymphocytes.
backHtml: Mycophenolate inhibits IMP dehydrogenase; lymphocytes depend on de novo guanine synthesis, so they are most affected.

frontHtml: Explain TB reactivation with TNF inhibitors through loss of granuloma maintenance.
backHtml: TNF keeps granulomas intact; TNF inhibitors reactivate latent TB, so screen and treat latent infection first.

frontHtml: Recognize PML from JC virus as a complication of rituximab and other immunosuppressive biologics.
backHtml: Subacute focal deficits with non-enhancing white-matter lesions on rituximab suggest PML from JC virus.

frontHtml: Recognize the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after treatment of syphilis and distinguish it from drug allergy.
backHtml: Fever and rigors hours after first treating syphilis are the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction from spirochete lysis, not penicillin allergy.

frontHtml: Apply the HIV testing algorithm to diagnose acute HIV infection.
backHtml: Reactive Ag/Ab screen + negative differentiation assay → HIV-1 RNA to diagnose acute infection.

frontHtml: Order HIV testing before starting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis.
backHtml: Exclude HIV infection before starting PrEP, because a PrEP regimen under-treats established HIV and selects for resistance.

frontHtml: Manage an occupational high-risk HIV exposure with prompt three-drug post-exposure prophylaxis.
backHtml: Start three-drug PEP as soon as possible (within 72 hours) after a high-risk exposure and continue it for 28 days; don't wait for results.

frontHtml: Choose opportunistic-infection prophylaxis from CD4 count and Toxoplasma serology in advanced HIV.
backHtml: CD4 <200 → PCP prophylaxis; CD4 <100 with Toxoplasma IgG → also toxo prophylaxis; daily TMP-SMX covers both.

frontHtml: Manage paradoxical TB-associated IRIS by continuing ART and TB therapy.
backHtml: Paradoxical IRIS: continue ART and the pathogen-directed therapy; treat the inflammation.

frontHtml: Start antiretroviral therapy immediately in pregnancy to prevent perinatal HIV transmission.
backHtml: Pregnancy with HIV: start ART immediately, without waiting for resistance results or a later trimester.

frontHtml: Evaluate a low-risk penicillin allergy label with a direct oral amoxicillin challenge.
backHtml: Low-risk penicillin allergy history (remote benign rash): direct oral amoxicillin challenge, then delabel.

frontHtml: Manage Stevens-Johnson syndrome by withdrawing the culprit drug and giving supportive inpatient care.
backHtml: SJS/TEN: stop the culprit immediately and give supportive care in a burn or intensive care unit.

frontHtml: Diagnose DRESS from timing, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement.
backHtml: Weeks after a new drug: fever, rash, facial edema, eosinophilia and organ injury = DRESS.

frontHtml: Advise early peanut introduction to prevent peanut allergy in a low-risk infant.
backHtml: Introduce peanut early (around 4–6 months) in infants with mild or no eczema, even with an allergic sibling.

frontHtml: Give intramuscular epinephrine first in anaphylaxis.
backHtml: Anaphylaxis: intramuscular epinephrine into the thigh first; everything else is adjunctive.

frontHtml: Plan discharge after anaphylaxis with epinephrine autoinjectors and allergy follow-up.
backHtml: Discharge after anaphylaxis: epinephrine autoinjectors (two), training, an action plan and allergist referral.

frontHtml: Treat syphilis in pregnancy with penicillin after desensitization when the patient has a true penicillin allergy.
backHtml: Syphilis in pregnancy with true penicillin allergy: desensitize and treat with penicillin.

frontHtml: Treat tissue-invasive CMV disease after solid-organ transplantation with ganciclovir.
backHtml: Tissue-invasive CMV after transplant: intravenous ganciclovir (valganciclovir for milder disease); foscarnet only for resistance.

frontHtml: Order an allograft biopsy for unexplained kidney transplant dysfunction after noninvasive evaluation.
backHtml: Unexplained rising creatinine in a kidney transplant after ultrasound, drug levels and BK testing → allograft biopsy.

frontHtml: Counsel solid-organ transplant recipients about their high risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.
backHtml: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is the most common cancer after solid-organ transplant; counsel sun protection and annual skin checks.

frontHtml: Recognize CYP3A4-inhibitor interactions that cause calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity.
backHtml: Clarithromycin (CYP3A4 inhibitor) raises tacrolimus levels; rifampin and other inducers lower them.

frontHtml: Schedule live vaccines before solid-organ transplantation in seronegative candidates.
backHtml: Give live vaccines to transplant candidates at least 4 weeks before transplant; they are contraindicated afterward.

frontHtml: Calculate the number needed to treat from event rates in a transplant prophylaxis trial.
backHtml: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction; here 1 / (0.20 − 0.10) = 10.

frontHtml: Draw conclusions from a trial summary that respect its primary outcome, harms and population.
backHtml: Conclude only what the primary outcome and reported harms support, within the enrolled population.

frontHtml: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting a TNF inhibitor.
backHtml: Before a TNF inhibitor: screen for latent TB (IGRA) and hepatitis B, and update vaccines.

frontHtml: Give hepatitis B antiviral prophylaxis to core antibody–positive patients receiving rituximab.
backHtml: Core antibody–positive patients starting rituximab need antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir or tenofovir), even if HBsAg is negative.

frontHtml: Manage severe immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis with drug interruption and glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Severe checkpoint-inhibitor colitis: hold the drug and give systemic glucocorticoids; add infliximab or vedolizumab if refractory.

frontHtml: Treat checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis by replacing glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone.
backHtml: Checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis: replace glucocorticoid first, then thyroid hormone; mineralocorticoid is not needed.

frontHtml: Reduce low-dose methotrexate adverse effects with folic acid supplementation.
backHtml: Methotrexate mucositis, nausea and mild ALT rise: add folic acid and continue the drug with monitoring.

frontHtml: Start bisphosphonate prophylaxis in a patient at high fracture risk who begins long-term glucocorticoids.
backHtml: Long-term glucocorticoids plus high fracture risk: start a bisphosphonate along with calcium and vitamin D.

frontHtml: Recommend recombinant zoster vaccine for adults immunosuppressed by biologic therapy.
backHtml: Immunosuppressed adults (including on TNF inhibitors) can and should get the non-live recombinant zoster vaccine.

frontHtml: Explain how cytoadherence of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes produces cerebral malaria.
backHtml: cerebral malaria results from PfEMP1-mediated cytoadherence and sequestration of P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes in cerebral microvessels.

frontHtml: Identify the Duffy antigen as the erythrocyte receptor used by Plasmodium vivax.
backHtml: P. vivax invades reticulocytes through the Duffy antigen; its hypnozoites explain relapse after blood-stage prophylaxis.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of action of chloroquine against blood-stage Plasmodium.
backHtml: chloroquine kills blood-stage parasites by preventing detoxification of heme into hemozoin.

frontHtml: Identify erythroid progenitors as the target of parvovirus B19 in aplastic crisis.
backHtml: parvovirus B19 infects erythroid progenitors; with chronic hemolysis this causes aplastic crisis with reticulocytopenia.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of hydrops fetalis caused by maternal parvovirus B19 infection.
backHtml: parvovirus B19 causes nonimmune hydrops fetalis through severe fetal anemia and high-output heart failure.

frontHtml: Relate the drug of choice for ehrlichiosis to its ribosomal mechanism.
backHtml: ehrlichiosis is treated with doxycycline, a 30S inhibitor that blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding.

frontHtml: Distinguish anaplasmosis from ehrlichiosis by the infected leukocyte and geography.
backHtml: morulae in neutrophils mean Anaplasma (Ixodes tick); morulae in monocytes mean Ehrlichia (lone star tick).

frontHtml: Identify Bartonella quintana as a louse-borne cause of culture-negative endocarditis.
backHtml: body lice plus culture-negative endocarditis points to Bartonella quintana.

frontHtml: Explain the initiating mechanism of disseminated intravascular coagulation in Gram-negative sepsis.
backHtml: in sepsis-associated DIC, cytokine- and endotoxin-induced tissue factor triggers widespread thrombin generation and consumption.

frontHtml: Identify the reactive CD8+ T cell as the atypical lymphocyte of EBV mononucleosis.
backHtml: the atypical lymphocytes of mononucleosis are reactive CD8+ T cells, not infected B cells.

frontHtml: Describe the nature and origin of heterophile antibodies in EBV infection.
backHtml: heterophile antibodies are non-EBV-specific IgM from polyclonal B-cell activation.

frontHtml: Explain referred shoulder-tip pain after splenic rupture in mononucleosis.
backHtml: shoulder-tip pain from splenic rupture is referred through the phrenic nerve (C3-C5).

frontHtml: Identify the latency site of cytomegalovirus after heterophile-negative mononucleosis.
backHtml: CMV, a cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis, stays latent in monocytes and myeloid progenitors.

frontHtml: Recognize the lymph node pattern and exposures of acute toxoplasmic lymphadenitis.
backHtml: follicular hyperplasia, epithelioid histiocyte clusters and monocytoid B cells in a posterior cervical node suggest toxoplasmosis.

frontHtml: Identify Bartonella henselae from the history and node histology of cat-scratch disease.
backHtml: regional adenitis weeks after a kitten scratch, with stellate necrotizing granulomas, means Bartonella henselae.

frontHtml: Contrast the acquisition of nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis with tuberculous lymphadenitis.
backHtml: nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis in toddlers comes from the environment through oropharyngeal mucosa, and excision is curative.

frontHtml: Explain the anatomic basis of acute lymphangitis and its regional nodal drainage.
backHtml: a tender red streak from a wound to the regional nodes is lymphangitis, usually streptococcal, spreading in superficial lymphatics.

frontHtml: Match reactive lymph node patterns to the compartment and immune cell involved.
backHtml: viral lymphadenitis causes paracortical (T-zone) hyperplasia with immunoblasts and preserved architecture.

frontHtml: Explain how impaired cytotoxic granule function produces the hyperinflammation of HLH.
backHtml: HLH arises when defective cytotoxic killing leaves T cells and macrophages chronically activated, with interferon-gamma as the central cytokine.

frontHtml: Identify activated interferon-gamma-producing T cells as the driver of EBV-triggered secondary HLH.
backHtml: secondary HLH is driven by interferon-gamma-secreting T cells; EBV is the classic trigger and soluble CD25 and ferritin are markers.

frontHtml: Explain the dissociation between ESR and other inflammatory markers in macrophage activation syndrome.
backHtml: in macrophage activation syndrome, fibrinogen consumption lowers the ESR while ferritin and CRP rise.

frontHtml: Attribute the systemic features of multicentric Castleman disease to interleukin-6.
backHtml: Castleman disease is an IL-6-driven lymphoproliferation; the multicentric form in HIV is caused by HHV-8.

frontHtml: Link defective FAS-mediated apoptosis to the findings of autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.
backHtml: ALPS is a FAS-pathway apoptosis defect marked by double-negative alpha-beta T cells, lymphoproliferation and autoimmune cytopenias.

frontHtml: Identify the cell of origin and markers of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
backHtml: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a CD1a/langerin-positive myeloid dendritic cell neoplasm with Birbeck granules and frequent BRAF V600E.

frontHtml: Recognize the histology and natural history of Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
backHtml: neutrophil-poor necrotizing lymphadenitis with karyorrhectic debris in a young adult is Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, which resolves spontaneously.

frontHtml: Explain the T-helper 1-dependent mechanism of non-necrotizing granuloma formation.
backHtml: sarcoid granulomas are a Th1/interferon-gamma-driven type IV response producing non-necrotizing epithelioid granulomas.

frontHtml: Differentiate reactive follicular hyperplasia from follicular lymphoma on nodal findings.
backHtml: reactive follicular hyperplasia is polymorphous and polyclonal with tingible-body macrophages; follicular lymphoma is monotonous, clonal and BCL2-positive.

frontHtml: Use TdT to establish lymphoblastic lineage in childhood acute leukemia.
backHtml: TdT positivity identifies lymphoblasts; CD10/CD19 without surface immunoglobulin indicates precursor B-cell disease.

frontHtml: Identify Auer rods as fused myeloperoxidase-containing granules in myeloid blasts.
backHtml: Auer rods are coalesced myeloperoxidase-rich primary granules and mark myeloid blasts; alkylating agents cause therapy-related AML with chromosome 5/7 loss.

frontHtml: Recognize the immunophenotype of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
backHtml: CLL is a CD5+ CD23+ monoclonal B-cell neoplasm; smudge cells and absolute lymphocytosis are the clues on the smear.

frontHtml: Explain ineffective hematopoiesis as the cause of cytopenias in myelodysplastic syndrome.
backHtml: myelodysplastic syndrome causes cytopenias despite a hypercellular marrow because dysplastic progenitors undergo apoptosis.

frontHtml: Connect t(11;14) and cyclin D1 overexpression to mantle cell lymphoma.
backHtml: mantle cell lymphoma is CD5+/CD23− with t(11;14) and cyclin D1 overexpression driving G1-S progression.

frontHtml: Describe how HTLV-1 Tax drives adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma.
backHtml: HTLV-1 Tax activates NF-kappa B and IL-2 signalling, producing CD4+ CD25+ adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma with hypercalcemia.

frontHtml: Select intravenous artesunate as treatment for severe falciparum malaria.
backHtml: severe falciparum malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate, followed by a complete oral combination course.

frontHtml: Order appropriate first-line testing for suspected malaria in a returning traveller.
backHtml: in a febrile returning traveller, order thick and thin smears plus a rapid antigen test at once, and repeat if negative.

frontHtml: Choose first-line therapy for uncomplicated babesiosis.
backHtml: treat uncomplicated babesiosis with atovaquone plus azithromycin; reserve clindamycin-quinine and exchange transfusion for severe disease.

frontHtml: Manage transient aplastic crisis in a child with sickle cell anemia.
backHtml: treat aplastic crisis with simple transfusion and isolation; erythropoiesis recovers as antibody appears.

frontHtml: Initiate empiric doxycycline for suspected anaplasmosis.
backHtml: treat suspected anaplasmosis or ehrlichiosis empirically with doxycycline without waiting for confirmation.

frontHtml: Manage sepsis-associated disseminated intravascular coagulation.
backHtml: treat the underlying cause of DIC; give blood products for bleeding, not to normalize laboratory values.

frontHtml: Counsel an athlete on return to play after infectious mononucleosis.
backHtml: after mononucleosis, hold contact sports for at least 3 weeks and until splenomegaly has resolved.

frontHtml: Interpret a negative heterophile test and choose confirmatory EBV serology.
backHtml: a heterophile-negative mononucleosis syndrome calls for EBV-specific serology, then CMV, HIV and toxoplasmosis testing.

frontHtml: Select management for regional cat-scratch lymphadenitis.
backHtml: azithromycin shortens bulky cat-scratch adenitis; aspirate rather than incise suppurative nodes.

frontHtml: Manage nontuberculous mycobacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a young child.
backHtml: excise nontuberculous mycobacterial cervical adenitis in children; use macrolide-based therapy when surgery is risky.

frontHtml: Triage persistent supraclavicular lymphadenopathy in an older adult.
backHtml: a fixed supraclavicular node in an older smoker needs cross-sectional imaging and tissue diagnosis, not observation or antibiotics.

frontHtml: Choose the biopsy approach for a high-risk lymph node when no primary tumour is found.
backHtml: sample a high-risk node with excisional or adequate core biopsy; aspiration cytology is not sufficient to classify lymphoma.

frontHtml: Evaluate suspected hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in an adult.
backHtml: ferritin in the thousands with fever, cytopenias and splenomegaly calls for urgent marrow evaluation and a search for an HLH trigger.

frontHtml: Diagnose macrophage activation syndrome from serial laboratory trends.
backHtml: in systemic JIA, falling platelets and fibrinogen with soaring ferritin mean macrophage activation syndrome, not a flare.

frontHtml: Select treatment for HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease.
backHtml: HHV-8-associated multicentric Castleman disease is treated with rituximab plus antiretroviral therapy; siltuximab is for the idiopathic form.

frontHtml: Manage multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis with pituitary involvement.
backHtml: multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis needs systemic chemotherapy, and its diabetes insipidus needs desmopressin.

frontHtml: Manage biopsy-proven Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
backHtml: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease needs supportive care and follow-up for later lupus, not antibiotics or chemotherapy.

frontHtml: Decide whether to treat asymptomatic sarcoidosis with hilar adenopathy.
backHtml: asymptomatic stage I sarcoidosis is observed with structured monitoring; steroids are for symptomatic or organ-threatening disease.

frontHtml: Decide when to start therapy in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
backHtml: asymptomatic early-stage CLL is observed; treat only for cytopenias, bulky or symptomatic disease, or constitutional symptoms.

frontHtml: Apply diagnostic criteria to distinguish MGUS, smoldering myeloma and myeloma.
backHtml: without a myeloma-defining event, a monoclonal gammopathy is monitored rather than treated.

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenström macroglobulinemia.
backHtml: symptomatic hyperviscosity in Waldenström macroglobulinemia is treated first with plasmapheresis, before systemic therapy.

frontHtml: Select JAK inhibitor therapy for symptomatic primary myelofibrosis.
backHtml: ruxolitinib relieves splenomegaly and symptoms in primary myelofibrosis; transplantation is the only cure.

frontHtml: Choose Helicobacter pylori eradication as first-line therapy for localized gastric MALT lymphoma.
backHtml: localized gastric MALT lymphoma with H. pylori is treated first by eradicating the infection, with endoscopic follow-up.

frontHtml: Choose tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis according to risk.
backHtml: high-risk tumor lysis prophylaxis is hydration plus rasburicase; allopurinol suits intermediate risk and cannot lower existing urate.

frontHtml: Explain the rationale for central nervous system prophylaxis in childhood ALL.
backHtml: central nervous system prophylaxis with intrathecal chemotherapy is given to every child with ALL because the meninges are a sanctuary site.

frontHtml: Select stage-appropriate therapy for mycosis fungoides.
backHtml: early-stage mycosis fungoides is treated with skin-directed therapy; Sézary syndrome is the erythrodermic leukemic variant.

frontHtml: Explain why Roux-en-Y gastric bypass causes iron deficiency anemia.
backHtml: after gastric bypass, microcytic anemia with a very low ferritin is usually malabsorptive iron deficiency.

frontHtml: Identify the enzyme whose inhibition by lead produces basophilic stippling.
backHtml: coarse basophilic stippling in lead poisoning reflects inhibited pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase.

frontHtml: Explain how nitrous oxide produces a B12-deficiency myelopathy despite a normal serum B12.
backHtml: recreational nitrous oxide causes functional B 12 deficiency by inactivating cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase.

frontHtml: Predict the gastric physiology of pernicious anemia.
backHtml: autoimmune gastritis gives achlorhydria with a high serum gastrin.

frontHtml: Diagnose pure red cell aplasia associated with thymoma.
backHtml: isolated anemia with absent reticulocytes and erythroid precursors plus an anterior mediastinal mass suggests thymoma-associated pure red cell aplasia.

frontHtml: Identify the renal cell type that produces erythropoietin.
backHtml: anemia of CKD reflects loss of erythropoietin-producing peritubular interstitial cells.

frontHtml: Relate the clinical triad of PNH to its molecular defect.
backHtml: PNH is a somatic stem cell defect in GPI-anchor synthesis that removes complement regulators.

frontHtml: Identify pyruvate kinase deficiency from its metabolic signature.
backHtml: Coombs-negative lifelong hemolysis with raised 2,3-BPG and normal G6PD suggests pyruvate kinase deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of extravascular hemolysis in warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
backHtml: warm AIHA destroys IgG-coated cells by Fc receptor-mediated splenic phagocytosis, producing spherocytes.

frontHtml: Distinguish the hapten mechanism of drug-induced immune hemolysis from other mechanisms.
backHtml: high-dose penicillin causes extravascular hemolysis by a hapten mechanism with an IgG-positive DAT.

frontHtml: Trace the renal handling of free hemoglobin in intravascular hemolysis.
backHtml: urine hemosiderin comes from shed proximal tubular cells that reabsorbed filtered free hemoglobin.

frontHtml: Explain why rasburicase causes oxidant hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
backHtml: rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and can trigger hemolysis and methemoglobinemia in G6PD deficiency.

frontHtml: Link functional asplenia in sickle cell disease to pneumococcal sepsis.
backHtml: functional asplenia in sickle cell disease brings the greatest risk from Streptococcus pneumoniae .

frontHtml: Explain why sickle trait causes hematuria and hyposthenuria.
backHtml: sickle trait cells sickle in the hypoxic, hypertonic, acidic renal medulla.

frontHtml: Identify hemoglobin C disease from its smear and electrophoresis.
backHtml: HbC (Glu6Lys) causes target cells, intracellular crystals and mild hemolysis.

frontHtml: Infer parental α-globin genotypes from a pregnancy affected by Hb Bart's hydrops.
backHtml: Hb Bart's hydrops arises when both parents carry the cis α-thalassemia deletion (−−/αα).

frontHtml: Locate the site of red cell destruction in hereditary spherocytosis.
