backHtml: spherocytes are trapped and destroyed in the splenic cords of the red pulp.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of hemin in acute intermittent porphyria.
backHtml: hemin treats acute porphyric attacks by negative feedback repression of hepatic ALA synthase.

frontHtml: Choose intravenous iron for iron deficiency anemia in active inflammatory bowel disease.
backHtml: give intravenous iron for iron deficiency in active IBD, especially with oral intolerance or hemoglobin below 10 g/dL.

frontHtml: Test for vitamin B12 deficiency in a patient taking metformin and a proton pump inhibitor.
backHtml: check B 12 in patients on long-term metformin or acid suppression who develop macrocytosis or neuropathy.

frontHtml: Treat pernicious anemia with neurologic involvement.
backHtml: treat pernicious anemia with neurologic signs with parenteral B 12 , lifelong.

frontHtml: Select definitive therapy for severe aplastic anemia in a young patient with a matched sibling donor.
backHtml: young patients with severe aplastic anemia and a matched sibling should proceed to allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

frontHtml: Treat persistent parvovirus B19 red cell aplasia in an immunocompromised patient.
backHtml: chronic parvovirus B19 red cell aplasia in an immunocompromised host is treated with IVIG and reduced immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Sequence iron repletion before ESA therapy in anemia of chronic kidney disease.
backHtml: in anemia of CKD, replete iron first and use ESAs only to modest hemoglobin targets.

frontHtml: Confirm a raised capillary blood lead level with venous testing.
backHtml: confirm a raised capillary blood lead level with a venous sample before acting on it.

frontHtml: Start glucocorticoids for newly diagnosed warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
backHtml: glucocorticoids are first-line therapy for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

frontHtml: Choose rituximab for steroid-dependent warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
backHtml: rituximab is the preferred second-line therapy for steroid-dependent or refractory warm AIHA.

frontHtml: Choose B-cell-directed therapy for symptomatic cold agglutinin disease.
backHtml: symptomatic primary cold agglutinin disease is treated with warming plus rituximab-based therapy, not steroids or splenectomy.

frontHtml: Order flow cytometry to diagnose paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
backHtml: test Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis with cytopenias by flow cytometry for PNH.

frontHtml: Vaccinate against meningococcus before starting complement C5 inhibition.
backHtml: vaccinate against meningococci (ACWY and B) at least 2 weeks before starting a C5 inhibitor.

frontHtml: Test G6PD activity before prescribing primaquine or tafenoquine.
backHtml: test G6PD activity before primaquine or tafenoquine radical cure.

frontHtml: Interpret a normal G6PD level during acute hemolysis.
backHtml: a normal G6PD level during acute hemolysis does not exclude deficiency; retest after recovery.

frontHtml: Manage drug-induced immune hemolysis by stopping the offending drug.
backHtml: stop the drug at once in suspected drug-induced immune hemolysis.

frontHtml: Start empiric antibiotics for acute chest syndrome.
backHtml: treat acute chest syndrome with a cephalosporin plus a macrolide, oxygen and incentive spirometry.

frontHtml: Choose exchange transfusion for severe acute chest syndrome.
backHtml: use exchange transfusion for severe or rapidly progressive acute chest syndrome.

frontHtml: Start hydroxyurea for recurrent vaso-occlusive complications of sickle cell disease.
backHtml: hydroxyurea is the core disease-modifying therapy after recurrent pain crises or acute chest syndrome.

frontHtml: Start chronic transfusion after an abnormal transcranial Doppler screen.
backHtml: a confirmed abnormal transcranial Doppler in sickle cell disease calls for chronic transfusion.

frontHtml: Treat fever in a child with sickle cell disease with prompt parenteral antibiotics.
backHtml: give prompt parenteral ceftriaxone for fever in a child with sickle cell disease.

frontHtml: Order α-globin gene analysis for suspected α-thalassemia trait before pregnancy.
backHtml: microcytosis with normal iron and normal HbA 2 calls for α-globin gene testing, especially before pregnancy.

frontHtml: Monitor the absolute neutrophil count during deferiprone therapy.
backHtml: deferiprone requires weekly neutrophil monitoring because of agranulocytosis.

frontHtml: Vaccinate before elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis.
backHtml: vaccinate against encapsulated organisms at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.

frontHtml: Treat an acute attack of acute intermittent porphyria.
backHtml: treat an acute porphyric attack with neurologic signs or hyponatremia with intravenous hemin.

frontHtml: Treat porphyria cutanea tarda with iron reduction.
backHtml: treat porphyria cutanea tarda with phlebotomy (or low-dose hydroxychloroquine) plus removal of triggers.

frontHtml: Explain why hemoglobin concentration is preserved immediately after acute whole-blood loss.
backHtml: an early normal hemoglobin does not exclude major hemorrhage; judge early loss by hemodynamics.

frontHtml: Predict the time course of the marrow response after acute blood loss.
backHtml: the reticulocyte response to acute blood loss appears after a few days and peaks at about a week.

frontHtml: Identify the membrane mechanism of spur cell anemia in advanced liver disease.
backHtml: acanthocytes with DAT-negative hemolysis in advanced cirrhosis mean spur cell anemia from membrane cholesterol excess.

frontHtml: Explain the formation of target cells in cholestatic liver disease.
backHtml: target cells form when membrane surface area rises relative to volume, as with membrane lipid loading in cholestatic liver disease.

frontHtml: Explain the dilutional fall in hemoglobin in normal pregnancy.
backHtml: the physiologic anemia of pregnancy is dilutional: plasma expands more than red cell mass.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of the physiologic anemia of infancy.
backHtml: the physiologic nadir of infancy results from suppressed erythropoietin after the rise in oxygenation at birth.

frontHtml: Explain how high cow's milk intake causes iron deficiency in toddlers.
backHtml: excess cow's milk causes toddler iron deficiency through low iron content, inhibition of absorption and displacement of iron-rich foods.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of anemia in hypothyroidism.
backHtml: hypothyroidism causes a mild hypoproliferative anemia through lower oxygen demand and less erythropoietin.

frontHtml: Recognise mixed nutritional anemia behind a normal MCV.
backHtml: a normal MCV with a high RDW and a dimorphic smear suggests mixed microcytic and macrocytic deficiencies.

frontHtml: Link the Duffy-null phenotype to benign neutropenia and resistance to vivax malaria.
backHtml: Duffy-null individuals have a benign lower neutrophil count and resist P. vivax invasion.

frontHtml: Identify the gene defect in cyclic neutropenia.
backHtml: cyclic neutropenia, with nadirs about every 21 days, is caused by autosomal dominant ELANE mutations.

frontHtml: Link agranulocytosis to the thionamide class and its mechanism of action.
backHtml: thionamides (thyroid peroxidase inhibitors) can cause agranulocytosis early in therapy; fever or sore throat warrants an immediate count.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of platelet destruction in childhood ITP.
backHtml: childhood ITP is post-viral IgG-mediated splenic clearance of platelets in a well child with an otherwise normal blood count.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of action of eltrombopag in chronic ITP.
backHtml: eltrombopag is an oral thrombopoietin-receptor agonist that must be taken apart from calcium and other polyvalent cations.

frontHtml: Explain the rapid action of intravenous immunoglobulin in ITP.
backHtml: IVIG raises the platelet count in ITP within days by blocking macrophage Fc receptors.

frontHtml: Distinguish neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia from other causes of neonatal thrombocytopenia.
backHtml: a thrombocytopenic well newborn with a normal maternal platelet count suggests alloimmune (NAIT) rather than maternal autoimmune thrombocytopenia.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanisms of thrombocytopenia in chronic liver disease.
backHtml: thrombocytopenia in cirrhosis results from splenic sequestration plus reduced hepatic thrombopoietin.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism and adverse effects of hydroxyurea in polycythemia vera.
backHtml: hydroxyurea, the usual cytoreductive drug for high-risk PV, inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and causes macrocytosis and leg ulcers.

frontHtml: Explain why iron deficiency develops and helps control the hematocrit in phlebotomy-treated PV.
backHtml: phlebotomy controls PV partly by inducing iron deficiency; microcytosis is the expected result and is not treated with iron.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of secondary erythrocytosis in smokers.
backHtml: smoker's erythrocytosis is driven by carboxyhemoglobin, which reduces oxygen delivery and raises erythropoietin despite a normal pulse oximetry reading.

frontHtml: Link VHL-related hemangioblastoma to erythropoietin-driven erythrocytosis.
backHtml: cerebellar hemangioblastoma can secrete erythropoietin; VHL loss stabilises HIF and drives EPO and VEGF.

frontHtml: Identify the driver mutations of essential thrombocythemia.
backHtml: in JAK2-negative essential thrombocythemia, a CALR mutation is the most likely driver.

frontHtml: Distinguish a leukemoid reaction from chronic myeloid leukemia.
backHtml: a leukemoid reaction shows toxic, mature neutrophils with a high LAP score, no basophilia and an obvious reactive cause.

frontHtml: Select targeted therapy for FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive hypereosinophilia.
backHtml: FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive hypereosinophilia is an imatinib-responsive tyrosine kinase-driven neoplasm.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of polycythemia in infants of diabetic mothers.
backHtml: infants of diabetic mothers develop polycythemia from hyperinsulinemia-driven fetal hypoxia and erythropoietin release.

frontHtml: Distinguish relative polycythemia from absolute erythrocytosis.
backHtml: relative polycythemia is a fall in plasma volume with a normal red cell mass, often from diuretics or dehydration.

frontHtml: Apply the restrictive transfusion threshold in stable upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
backHtml: transfuse stable upper GI bleeding patients without cardiovascular disease only below 7 g/dL.

frontHtml: Apply the transfusion threshold for an older adult with cardiovascular disease after orthopedic surgery.
backHtml: in stable patients with cardiovascular disease or after orthopedic surgery, transfuse one unit at a time when hemoglobin is below about 8 g/dL.

frontHtml: Manage cow's milk-associated iron deficiency in a toddler.
backHtml: treat toddler iron deficiency with milk limitation and oral iron, and confirm by a hemoglobin rise in 4 weeks.

frontHtml: Choose intravenous iron for oral-iron-refractory iron deficiency in late pregnancy.
backHtml: use intravenous iron in the second or third trimester when oral iron fails or is not tolerated.

frontHtml: Recognise athletes' pseudoanemia and limit testing.
backHtml: a mildly low hemoglobin with normal indices and ferritin in an endurance athlete is dilutional pseudoanemia.

frontHtml: Manage spur cell anemia in advanced cirrhosis.
backHtml: spur cell anemia marks end-stage cirrhosis; refer for liver transplant evaluation.

frontHtml: Select the recommended initial tests for suspected ITP in an adult.
backHtml: test adults with suspected ITP for HIV and hepatitis C; a marrow biopsy is not routinely needed.

frontHtml: Choose initial treatment for newly diagnosed adult ITP.
backHtml: first-line therapy for newly diagnosed adult ITP with platelets below 30,000/mm 3 or bleeding is a short course of glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Choose second-line therapy for steroid-dependent adult ITP.
backHtml: for steroid-dependent adult ITP within the first year, add a TPO-receptor agonist rather than continuing steroids or performing splenectomy.

frontHtml: Recognise and manage gestational thrombocytopenia.
backHtml: mild third-trimester thrombocytopenia with normal earlier counts and no other findings is gestational and needs only monitoring.

frontHtml: Select the definitive test for unexplained macrocytic pancytopenia in an older adult.
backHtml: after excluding nutritional and drug causes, unexplained pancytopenia, especially with dysplasia, needs a marrow biopsy with cytogenetics.

frontHtml: Manage severe neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia.
backHtml: treat severe neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia promptly with platelet transfusion, without waiting for antigen-matched units.

frontHtml: Manage low-risk polycythemia vera.
backHtml: treat low-risk PV with phlebotomy to hematocrit below 45% and low-dose aspirin.

frontHtml: Manage expected iron deficiency during phlebotomy for polycythemia vera.
backHtml: do not give iron for phlebotomy-induced iron deficiency in PV; it is part of the treatment.

frontHtml: Choose the next diagnostic step for suspected sleep apnea-related erythrocytosis.
backHtml: evaluate secondary erythrocytosis with normal daytime saturation for nocturnal hypoxemia from sleep apnea.

frontHtml: Prevent Strongyloides hyperinfection before glucocorticoid therapy in a patient with eosinophilia.
backHtml: give empiric ivermectin before high-dose steroids when Strongyloides exposure is possible and results are pending.

frontHtml: Confirm suspected neonatal polycythemia with a venous hematocrit.
backHtml: confirm a high neonatal capillary hematocrit with a venous sample before acting.

frontHtml: Recognise acquired von Willebrand syndrome in extreme thrombocytosis before antiplatelet therapy.
backHtml: check von Willebrand factor activity before aspirin in essential thrombocythemia with platelets above about 1 million/mm 3 .

frontHtml: Identify Bernard-Soulier syndrome as GpIb-IX-V deficiency from giant platelets and an uncorrected ristocetin defect.
backHtml: absent ristocetin response plus large platelets and no correction with normal plasma means a GpIb defect, not von Willebrand disease.

frontHtml: Localize Glanzmann thrombasthenia to failed fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation via GpIIb/IIIa.
backHtml: aggregation absent to all agonists but ristocetin = GpIIb/IIIa defect (Glanzmann).

frontHtml: Recognize factor XII deficiency as a cause of a prolonged aPTT without clinical bleeding.
backHtml: long aPTT that corrects with mixing in a person who has never bled points to factor XII deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the role of vitamin K in γ-carboxylation of clotting factors in a patient with acquired deficiency.
backHtml: vitamin K enables γ-carboxylation of glutamate; antibiotics plus no intake can deplete it within days to weeks.

frontHtml: Recognize that factor VIII is preserved in liver disease because it is produced by endothelial cells.
backHtml: factor VIII stays normal or high in liver disease and falls in DIC.

frontHtml: Identify factor XIII deficiency from normal coagulation screening, umbilical bleeding and a urea-soluble clot.
backHtml: normal screening tests plus umbilical bleeding and urea-soluble clot = factor XIII deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain acquired hemophilia A as a time-dependent autoantibody against factor VIII.
backHtml: a time-dependent inhibitor on mixing in a previously normal adult with new bleeding is an autoantibody to factor VIII.

frontHtml: Identify tissue factor expression as the trigger of sepsis-associated DIC.
backHtml: sepsis-associated DIC is driven by tissue factor expression, not by the contact pathway.

frontHtml: Explain that the prothrombin G20210A variant increases plasma prothrombin concentration.
backHtml: prothrombin G20210A raises the amount of a normal protein; factor V Leiden changes the protein's resistance to inactivation.

frontHtml: Link heparin resistance in nephrotic syndrome to urinary loss of antithrombin.
backHtml: heparin resistance with nephrotic syndrome points to urinary antithrombin loss.

frontHtml: Describe the anticoagulant action of activated protein C and the presentation of its homozygous deficiency.
backHtml: activated protein C cleaves Va and VIIIa; complete deficiency causes neonatal purpura fulminans.

frontHtml: Explain the in vitro prolongation of the aPTT by lupus anticoagulant despite a prothrombotic state.
backHtml: the lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT in the tube but causes clots in the patient.

frontHtml: State the mechanism of apixaban as a direct factor Xa inhibitor.
backHtml: the "-xaban" drugs are direct factor Xa inhibitors.

frontHtml: Explain how oral estrogen increases venous thrombosis risk.
backHtml: oral estrogen promotes VTE mainly by increasing hepatic procoagulant production and reducing natural anticoagulant activity.

frontHtml: Recognize Trousseau syndrome as cancer-associated hypercoagulability driven by tumor procoagulants.
backHtml: migratory superficial thrombophlebitis is a clue to visceral adenocarcinoma, especially pancreatic.

frontHtml: Explain the immune mechanism of an acute ABO hemolytic transfusion reaction.
backHtml: ABO-incompatible transfusion causes intravascular hemolysis through complement-fixing IgM isohemagglutinins.

frontHtml: Identify anti-IgA antibodies in IgA deficiency as the cause of transfusion-associated anaphylaxis.
backHtml: anaphylaxis at the start of a transfusion in a patient with IgA deficiency is caused by recipient anti-IgA antibodies.

frontHtml: Explain a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction as an anamnestic IgG alloantibody response.
backHtml: hemolysis 3–14 days after transfusion with a new alloantibody (often Kidd) is an anamnestic IgG response.

frontHtml: Identify irradiation as the product modification that prevents transfusion-associated GVHD.
backHtml: irradiate cellular blood products for profoundly immunosuppressed recipients to prevent TA-GVHD.

frontHtml: Explain the immune mechanism of TRALI and distinguish it from circulatory overload.
backHtml: TRALI = donor anti-leukocyte antibodies + primed recipient neutrophils = noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.

frontHtml: Explain citrate-induced hypocalcemia during massive transfusion.
backHtml: citrate in stored blood causes hypocalcemia during massive transfusion.

frontHtml: Explain why platelet products carry the highest risk of septic transfusion reactions.
backHtml: room-temperature storage makes platelets the blood component most often contaminated with bacteria.

frontHtml: Treat uremic platelet dysfunction bleeding with desmopressin.
backHtml: for acute uremic bleeding, give desmopressin; dialysis and anemia correction improve platelet function over time.

frontHtml: Treat an acute hemarthrosis in severe hemophilia A with immediate factor VIII replacement.
backHtml: in hemophilia, give the missing factor first and investigate later.

frontHtml: Treat bleeding in hemophilia A with a high-titer inhibitor using a bypassing agent.
backHtml: hemophilia with a high-titer inhibitor and active bleeding needs a bypassing agent, not more factor VIII.

frontHtml: Treat late vitamin K deficiency bleeding in an infant who missed prophylaxis.
backHtml: late vitamin K deficiency bleeding presents as intracranial hemorrhage in unprophylaxed breastfed infants; treat with vitamin K plus rapid factor replacement.

frontHtml: Choose cryoprecipitate for bleeding DIC with persistent hypofibrinogenemia.
backHtml: in bleeding DIC, replace fibrinogen with cryoprecipitate when it stays below about 150 mg/dL.

frontHtml: Avoid prophylactic blood products before paracentesis in cirrhosis despite an elevated INR.
backHtml: do not correct the INR or platelet count before paracentesis in cirrhosis.

frontHtml: Diagnose and treat scurvy as a cause of bleeding with normal coagulation tests.
backHtml: bleeding with normal coagulation tests and perifollicular hemorrhages suggests vitamin C deficiency.

frontHtml: Choose compression ultrasonography when DVT is likely by pretest probability.
backHtml: DVT likely by Wells → ultrasound; DVT unlikely → D-dimer first.

frontHtml: Select a direct oral anticoagulant as first-line treatment for uncomplicated proximal DVT.
backHtml: a DOAC is first-line for most patients with acute DVT.

frontHtml: Recommend extended-duration anticoagulation after a first unprovoked proximal DVT with low bleeding risk.
backHtml: unprovoked proximal VTE with low bleeding risk → extended anticoagulation; provoked by a major transient factor → 3 months.

frontHtml: Use a D-dimer as the first test when pretest probability of DVT is low.
backHtml: low pretest probability of DVT → D-dimer first; negative D-dimer ends the workup.

frontHtml: Choose low-molecular-weight heparin to treat VTE during pregnancy.
backHtml: treat VTE in pregnancy with LMWH; avoid warfarin and DOACs.

frontHtml: Select warfarin over DOACs for anticoagulation with a mechanical heart valve.
backHtml: mechanical valve → warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated.

frontHtml: Avoid thrombophilia testing after VTE provoked by a major transient risk factor.
backHtml: do not test for thrombophilia after VTE provoked by surgery; results will not change management.

frontHtml: Calculate the number needed to treat from event rates in a trial of extended anticoagulation.
backHtml: NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction, rounded up.

frontHtml: Judge the external validity of a trial by comparing a patient with its enrollment criteria.
backHtml: apply trial results to patients who meet the trial's inclusion and exclusion criteria.

frontHtml: Manage a mild urticarial transfusion reaction by pausing, giving an antihistamine and resuming.
backHtml: hives alone → pause, antihistamine, resume; anything more → stop.

frontHtml: Recognize and treat transfusion-associated circulatory overload in an older adult with heart failure.
backHtml: TACO (hypertension, high BNP, congestion) responds to diuretics; TRALI (hypotension, normal filling pressures) does not.

frontHtml: Stop the transfusion immediately when an acute hemolytic reaction is suspected.
backHtml: for any serious transfusion reaction, stop the transfusion first.

frontHtml: Apply balanced 1:1:1 blood product resuscitation in traumatic hemorrhagic shock.
backHtml: in massive hemorrhage, give products in a balanced ratio early and limit crystalloid.

frontHtml: Treat citrate-induced hypocalcemia after massive transfusion with intravenous calcium.
backHtml: check and replace ionized calcium during and after massive transfusion, especially with refractory hypotension.

frontHtml: Apply the prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold in chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia.
backHtml: chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia below 10,000/mm 3 → prophylactic platelets.

frontHtml: Apply a restrictive red cell transfusion threshold in a stable critically ill patient.
backHtml: stable inpatients without cardiovascular disease are transfused at hemoglobin below 7 g/dL, one unit at a time.

frontHtml: Manage a suspected septic transfusion reaction with cultures and empiric antibiotics.
backHtml: fever with hypotension during platelet transfusion → stop, culture patient and bag, start antibiotics.

frontHtml: Explain how chronic intravascular hemolysis from a prosthetic valve produces iron deficiency.
backHtml: chronic intravascular hemolysis, as with a leaking prosthetic valve, causes iron deficiency through hemoglobinuria and hemosiderinuria.

frontHtml: Identify exertional (march) hemoglobinuria as mechanical red-cell injury and distinguish it from rhabdomyolysis.
backHtml: transient hemoglobinuria after prolonged marching or running with normal CK is mechanical hemolysis in the soles; cushioned footwear prevents it.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of caplacizumab in immune TTP.
backHtml: caplacizumab blocks vWF A1-GPIb binding, the adhesion step that drives microthrombi in TTP.

frontHtml: Relate the mechanism of Shiga toxin to the pathogenesis of hemolytic uremic syndrome.
backHtml: Shiga toxin inactivates the 60S ribosome by depurinating 28S rRNA, injuring glomerular endothelium and causing HUS.

frontHtml: Identify factor H dysregulation as a cause of complement-mediated HUS.
backHtml: complement-mediated HUS reflects alternative-pathway dysregulation, most often of factor H; ADAMTS13 is not severely reduced.

frontHtml: Use coagulation tests to distinguish disseminated intravascular coagulation from TTP and HUS.
backHtml: consumption of fibrinogen and clotting factors (low fibrinogen, long PT/aPTT) separates DIC from TTP and HUS.

frontHtml: Explain haptoglobin depletion as the marker of intravascular hemolysis in device-related shear injury.
backHtml: haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is consumed in intravascular hemolysis; hemopexin binds free heme.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of thermal red-cell injury after extensive burns.
backHtml: severe burns cause thermal hemolysis with microspherocytes and fragments from heat-denatured spectrin.

frontHtml: Identify the target of rituximab and its role in immune TTP.
backHtml: rituximab targets CD20 on B cells and lowers relapse in immune TTP by reducing anti-ADAMTS13 antibody production.

frontHtml: Explain shear-induced loss of large von Willebrand multimers in aortic stenosis and assist devices.
backHtml: high shear from aortic stenosis or an LVAD unfolds vWF so that ADAMTS13 removes the largest multimers, causing acquired von Willebrand syndrome.

frontHtml: Explain why loss of the splenic marginal zone predisposes to encapsulated bacterial sepsis.
backHtml: the marginal zone of the spleen clears encapsulated bacteria and makes anti-polysaccharide IgM, which is why asplenia predisposes to pneumococcal sepsis.

frontHtml: Identify the contents of the splenorenal ligament and the risk to the pancreatic tail during splenectomy.
backHtml: the tail of the pancreas lies in the splenorenal ligament with the splenic vessels and is at risk during splenectomy.

frontHtml: Link functional asplenia in sickle cell disease to capsule-mediated pneumococcal virulence.
backHtml: the pneumococcal polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor exploited in functional asplenia of sickle cell disease.

frontHtml: Recognize celiac disease as a cause of functional hyposplenism with Howell-Jolly bodies.
backHtml: celiac disease can cause functional hyposplenism, recognized by Howell-Jolly bodies and a small spleen.

frontHtml: Explain hypersplenism from portal hypertension as a cause of pancytopenia with a normal marrow.
backHtml: hypersplenism from portal hypertension causes cytopenias with a normal marrow through splenic pooling and destruction.

frontHtml: Identify visceral leishmaniasis as a cause of massive splenomegaly and name its vector.
backHtml: visceral leishmaniasis, spread by sand flies, causes massive splenomegaly with pancytopenia and amastigotes in macrophages.

frontHtml: Explain referred left shoulder pain after splenic rupture.
backHtml: diaphragmatic irritation from splenic rupture refers pain to the left shoulder through the phrenic nerve.

frontHtml: Describe the gross and microscopic pathology of a splenic infarct.
backHtml: splenic infarcts are wedge-shaped, pale and show coagulative necrosis, the pattern of ischemia in solid organs except the brain.

frontHtml: Identify the embryologic origin of the spleen and the significance of accessory splenic tissue.
backHtml: the spleen arises from mesoderm in the dorsal mesogastrium; unfused buds become accessory spleens that can cause ITP relapse after splenectomy.

frontHtml: Explain how CYP2C19 loss-of-function alleles reduce clopidogrel efficacy.
backHtml: CYP2C19 poor metabolizers cannot activate the prodrug clopidogrel, increasing stent thrombosis risk.

frontHtml: Match the dabigatran reversal agent to its mechanism.
backHtml: idarucizumab, a Fab that binds dabigatran, is the specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

frontHtml: Distinguish direct factor Xa inhibitors from antithrombin-dependent and vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants.
backHtml: oral direct factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) inhibit free and prothrombinase-bound Xa without antithrombin.

frontHtml: Explain the pathophysiology of benzocaine-induced methemoglobinemia.
backHtml: methemoglobin (ferric heme) cannot carry oxygen and left-shifts the curve; suspect it with cyanosis, normal PaO2 and SpO2 near 85% after an oxidant drug.

frontHtml: Explain why rasburicase causes hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
backHtml: rasburicase generates hydrogen peroxide and is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia.
backHtml: drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia is caused by drug-dependent antibodies against platelet glycoproteins and causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

frontHtml: Distinguish hapten, immune-complex and autoantibody mechanisms of drug-induced hemolysis.
backHtml: high-dose penicillin causes hapten-type immune hemolysis: IgG-positive DAT, extravascular, drug-coated cells only.

frontHtml: Recognize TTP in pregnancy and begin plasma exchange rather than delivery.
backHtml: suspected TTP in pregnancy is treated with urgent plasma exchange, not delivery; normal BP and liver tests argue against HELLP.

frontHtml: Choose transesophageal echocardiography to evaluate suspected paravalvular leak hemolysis.
backHtml: new hemolysis and a regurgitant murmur after mechanical valve replacement suggest a paravalvular leak; TEE is the test of choice.

frontHtml: Vaccinate against meningococcus before starting C5 inhibitor therapy for complement-mediated HUS.
backHtml: vaccinate against meningococcus (ACWY and B) before C5 inhibitor therapy, adding antibiotic prophylaxis if treatment cannot wait.

frontHtml: Manage exertional hemoglobinuria with reassurance and preventive measures.
backHtml: exertional hemoglobinuria with normal CK and blood counts needs reassurance and better cushioning, not invasive tests.

frontHtml: Diagnose Shiga toxin-associated HUS from its triad and prodrome.
backHtml: MAHA, thrombocytopenia and AKI a week after bloody diarrhea in a young child is STEC-HUS.

frontHtml: Identify indications for dialysis in Shiga toxin-associated HUS.
backHtml: dialysis is indicated in STEC-HUS for refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, fluid overload or prolonged anuria.

frontHtml: Plan long-term kidney follow-up after Shiga toxin-associated HUS.
backHtml: after STEC-HUS, especially when dialysis was needed, follow blood pressure, proteinuria and kidney function long term.

frontHtml: Time vaccination at least 2 weeks before elective splenectomy.
backHtml: vaccinate at least 2 weeks before an elective splenectomy.

frontHtml: Select the vaccines indicated after emergency splenectomy.
backHtml: after emergency splenectomy, give pneumococcal conjugate, MenACWY, MenB and Hib vaccines about 2 weeks postoperatively.

frontHtml: Give immediate empiric IV antibiotics for fever in an asplenic patient.
backHtml: fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency: cultures, then immediate IV ceftriaxone (with vancomycin if septic) without waiting for tests.

frontHtml: Prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis after an animal bite in an asplenic patient.
backHtml: give amoxicillin-clavulanate after a dog or cat bite in an asplenic patient to cover Capnocytophaga and Pasteurella.

frontHtml: Manage acute splenic sequestration crisis in a child with sickle cell disease.
backHtml: acute splenic sequestration is treated with prompt, modest-volume simple red cell transfusion.

frontHtml: Choose CT with contrast for a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected splenic injury.
backHtml: in a hemodynamically stable patient with a positive FAST, CT with IV contrast guides nonoperative management of splenic injury.

frontHtml: Advise on return to contact sports after infectious mononucleosis.
backHtml: after mononucleosis, avoid contact sports for at least 3 to 4 weeks from symptom onset and until the spleen is no longer enlarged.

frontHtml: Investigate ITP relapse after splenectomy for an accessory spleen.
backHtml: ITP relapse after splenectomy with no Howell-Jolly bodies suggests an accessory spleen; locate it with heat-damaged red-cell scintigraphy.

frontHtml: Reverse warfarin with IV vitamin K and 4-factor PCC for intracranial hemorrhage.
backHtml: for warfarin-associated major bleeding, give IV vitamin K plus 4-factor PCC.

frontHtml: Choose idarucizumab to reverse dabigatran in life-threatening bleeding.
backHtml: reverse dabigatran in life-threatening bleeding with idarucizumab; kidney impairment prolongs its effect.

frontHtml: Calculate the ANC and manage afebrile chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.
backHtml: afebrile neutropenia in a well patient needs fever precautions, not empiric antibiotics or extra G-CSF.

frontHtml: Respond to fever and sore throat in a patient taking a thionamide.
backHtml: fever or sore throat on a thionamide: stop the drug and check a CBC with differential immediately.

frontHtml: Treat symptomatic benzocaine-induced methemoglobinemia with methylene blue.
backHtml: give IV methylene blue for symptomatic acquired methemoglobinemia when G6PD activity is normal.

frontHtml: Choose allopurinol over rasburicase for tumor lysis prevention in G6PD deficiency.
backHtml: in G6PD deficiency, prevent tumor lysis with hydration and allopurinol; rasburicase is contraindicated.

frontHtml: Manage drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia by stopping the drug and substituting an alternative.
backHtml: suspected drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia: stop the drug and substitute an unrelated agent.

frontHtml: Reverse unfractionated heparin with protamine sulfate.
backHtml: protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanisms of physiologic unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a term newborn.
backHtml: physiologic newborn jaundice is unconjugated, appears after 24 hours and reflects immature UGT1A1 plus increased bilirubin production.

frontHtml: Explain the timing of the physiologic IgG nadir in infancy.
backHtml: the 3–6-month IgG nadir is physiologic: maternal IgG has been catabolised and infant synthesis is still low.

frontHtml: Identify vitamin D supplementation as the measure that prevents nutritional rickets in breastfed infants.
backHtml: breastfed infants need 400 IU of vitamin D daily from the first days of life to prevent nutritional rickets.

frontHtml: Explain how excessive cow's milk intake causes iron deficiency anemia in a toddler.
backHtml: excess cow's milk causes toddler iron deficiency by low iron content, inhibited absorption, food displacement and occult blood loss.

frontHtml: Relate persistence of primitive reflexes to loss of descending cortical inhibition.
backHtml: primitive reflexes that persist beyond 6 months with spasticity point to an upper motor neuron lesion such as cerebral palsy.

frontHtml: Estimate a child's age from milestones across motor, language and social domains.
backHtml: a typical 3-year-old pedals a tricycle, copies a circle and speaks in three-word sentences that strangers mostly understand.

frontHtml: Distinguish the causes of in-toeing by age and examination findings.
backHtml: in-toeing at 3–8 years with inward-pointing kneecaps and excess hip internal rotation is femoral anteversion.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of postnatal ductus arteriosus closure.
backHtml: the ductus closes after birth because arterial oxygen rises and prostaglandin E2 falls; PGE1 infusion reverses this, COX inhibitors promote it.

frontHtml: Describe the source and structure of the protective antibody in human milk.
backHtml: breast milk protects the infant gut mainly with secretory IgA from mammary plasma cells primed in the mother's gut.

frontHtml: Identify ABO hemolytic disease as a cause of jaundice in the first day of life.
backHtml: jaundice before 24 hours with an O mother, an A or B infant and a positive antiglobulin test is ABO isoimmune hemolysis from maternal IgG.

frontHtml: Explain why continuous GnRH agonist therapy suppresses the reproductive axis.
backHtml: continuous GnRH agonist exposure downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors after an initial flare; pulsatile GnRH stimulates.

frontHtml: Distinguish adrenarche from gonadarche by its hormonal source.
backHtml: adrenarche reflects zona reticularis DHEA/DHEA-S production and is independent of the gonadotropin axis.

frontHtml: Identify the first sign of male puberty and the tissue that produces it.
backHtml: testicular enlargement is the first sign of male puberty and mostly reflects growth of the seminiferous tubules.

frontHtml: Explain the role of estrogen in pubertal growth-plate closure in males.
backHtml: estrogen made by aromatase drives epiphyseal fusion in both sexes; its absence in men leads to tall stature with open growth plates.

frontHtml: Explain the hormonal basis of normal pubertal gynecomastia.
backHtml: pubertal gynecomastia reflects a temporary rise in estrogen relative to androgen and usually regresses without treatment.

frontHtml: Explain the physiology of sleep-phase delay in adolescence.
backHtml: adolescent sleep-phase delay reflects a later circadian rhythm (later melatonin onset), not reduced sleep need.

frontHtml: Describe the mismatch in brain maturation that underlies adolescent risk-taking.
backHtml: adolescent risk-taking reflects early reward-system sensitivity outpacing the slower maturation of prefrontal control.

frontHtml: Explain how energy deficiency suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
backHtml: low leptin from low energy stores slows GnRH pulses and causes functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

frontHtml: Identify the earliest hormonal change of gonadarche.
backHtml: gonadarche begins with sleep-entrained increases in LH pulse amplitude, before any physical change.

frontHtml: Relate menarche to the timing of the female pubertal growth spurt.
backHtml: menarche occurs after peak height velocity, so girls have only limited growth left once periods begin.

frontHtml: Interpret a newborn pulse oximetry screen and choose the next step after a failed result.
backHtml: persistent newborn saturations below 95% at both sites on repeat screening are a failed CCHD screen: obtain an echocardiogram.

frontHtml: Choose diagnostic audiologic evaluation after a failed newborn hearing rescreen.
backHtml: an infant who fails the hearing screen and rescreen needs a diagnostic audiology evaluation (ABR) before 3 months of age.

frontHtml: Recognize false contraindications to routine infant vaccination.
backHtml: mild illness, low-grade fever and current antibiotics are not reasons to defer vaccination.

frontHtml: Identify the true contraindications to rotavirus vaccine.
backHtml: history of intussusception (or SCID) contraindicates rotavirus vaccine; other vaccines proceed.

frontHtml: Apply catch-up immunization principles to an interrupted infant series.
backHtml: in catch-up immunization, give the next dose and continue at minimum intervals; never restart a series.

frontHtml: Use the pattern of growth curves to direct the evaluation of growth faltering.
backHtml: in growth faltering with weight falling first and head growth preserved, start with a detailed feeding and diet history.

frontHtml: Choose first-line management for obesity in a school-age child.
backHtml: children 6 years and older with obesity should be offered intensive, family-based behavioural treatment (26+ contact hours) now.

frontHtml: Give current car-seat guidance for a toddler.
backHtml: keep toddlers rear-facing until they reach their seat's rear-facing height or weight limit, not until a fixed age.

frontHtml: Choose fluoride varnish as routine caries prevention in primary care.
backHtml: apply fluoride varnish in primary care from first tooth eruption through age 5; oral fluoride only if water is deficient.

frontHtml: Identify the age and method of universal pediatric lipid screening.
backHtml: screen all children for dyslipidemia once at 9–11 years (nonfasting is acceptable) and again at 17–21 years.

frontHtml: Set up a confidential adolescent psychosocial interview.
backHtml: explain confidentiality and its limits to parent and adolescent, then interview the adolescent alone.

frontHtml: Choose the appropriate STI screening test for an asymptomatic sexually active adolescent.
backHtml: screen sexually active females under 25 yearly for chlamydia and gonorrhea with a vaginal swab NAAT; no cytology before 21.

frontHtml: Recommend long-acting reversible contraception as first-line for an adolescent.
backHtml: LARC, such as the etonogestrel implant, is first-line contraception for adolescents; pair it with condoms for STI prevention.

frontHtml: Choose suicide risk assessment as the next step after a positive adolescent depression screen.
backHtml: after a positive adolescent depression screen, ask directly about suicidal ideation, plan and means before anything else.

frontHtml: Recognize when imminent risk of harm overrides adolescent confidentiality.
backHtml: an adolescent with an active suicide plan needs emergency evaluation and parental notification; imminent risk overrides confidentiality.

frontHtml: Diagnose constitutional delay of growth and puberty from growth data and laboratory results.
backHtml: constitutional delay shows normal growth velocity, delayed bone age, prepubertal gonadotropins and often a family history of late puberty.

frontHtml: Choose karyotype in a girl with delayed puberty and elevated gonadotropins.
backHtml: delayed puberty with high FSH means gonadal failure; in a short girl obtain a karyotype for Turner syndrome.

frontHtml: Choose brain imaging in a boy with central precocious puberty.
backHtml: every boy with central precocious puberty needs a brain MRI to look for a CNS lesion.

frontHtml: Recognize pre-participation findings that require cardiac evaluation before sports clearance.
backHtml: exertional syncope or presyncope, family history of early sudden death or a dynamic murmur means no sports clearance until cardiac evaluation.

frontHtml: Identify medical instability requiring hospital admission in an adolescent eating disorder.
backHtml: an adolescent with an eating disorder and bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia or electrolyte disturbance needs inpatient medical stabilization.

frontHtml: Time live vaccine administration after high-dose corticosteroid therapy.
backHtml: after high-dose steroids for 14 days or more, wait at least 1 month after stopping before giving a live vaccine.

frontHtml: Manage risky adolescent alcohol use found on screening.
backHtml: screen-positive risky adolescent substance use is managed with a motivational brief intervention, a safety plan and follow-up.

frontHtml: Explain why FSH rises more than LH after menopause.
backHtml: Postmenopausal FSH rises more than LH because the failing ovary loses both inhibin B and estradiol feedback.

frontHtml: Identify neurokinin B and the NK3 receptor as the mechanism of menopausal vasomotor symptoms.
backHtml: Postmenopausal hot flashes are driven by neurokinin B signalling through NK3 receptors, the target of fezolinetant.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of bone loss after estrogen withdrawal.
backHtml: Estrogen deficiency causes bone loss by raising the RANKL-to-osteoprotegerin ratio and boosting osteoclast activity.

frontHtml: Identify peripheral aromatization in adipose tissue as the source of postmenopausal estrone.
backHtml: Postmenopausal estrogen is mainly estrone made by aromatase in adipose tissue from adrenal and ovarian androstenedione.

frontHtml: Relate low adult bone density to failure to reach peak bone mass after adolescent amenorrhea.
backHtml: Peak bone mass is set by about age 30; adolescent hypoestrogenism and undernutrition lower it permanently.

frontHtml: Explain the main physiologic cause of declining maximal oxygen uptake with age.
backHtml: The age-related fall in VO 2 max is driven mainly by a falling maximal heart rate, which training does not prevent.

frontHtml: Identify the autonomic pathway and mediator responsible for erection.
backHtml: Erection depends on parasympathetic nitric oxide and cGMP; emission is sympathetic and ejaculation is pudendal.

frontHtml: Contrast male reproductive aging with female menopause.
backHtml: Male reproductive aging is a gradual fall in free testosterone with rising SHBG and preserved spermatogenesis.

frontHtml: Distinguish normal bereavement from depression and prolonged grief disorder.
backHtml: Early grief with intact self-worth and returning function is normal bereavement; it needs support and follow-up, not psychiatric diagnosis.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of raised vaginal pH in genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
backHtml: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause raises vaginal pH because estrogen loss depletes epithelial glycogen and lactobacilli.

frontHtml: Explain why serum creatinine overestimates kidney function in older adults.
backHtml: In small, older adults a normal creatinine can hide a low GFR; dose renally cleared drugs by estimated clearance.

frontHtml: Explain why older adults develop hypernatremia during dehydrating illness.
backHtml: Reduced thirst and lower body water make older adults prone to hypernatremia when water losses rise.

frontHtml: Explain the physiologic basis of orthostatic hypotension in older adults.
backHtml: Blunted baroreflex sensitivity is a normal age-related change that predisposes older adults to orthostatic hypotension.

frontHtml: Predict the effect of normal aging on lung volumes.
backHtml: With aging, loss of elastic recoil raises residual volume while total lung capacity stays about the same.

frontHtml: Localize the lesion in age-related hearing loss.
backHtml: Presbycusis is high-frequency sensorineural loss from hair cell loss at the cochlear base.

frontHtml: Link immunosenescence of T-cell immunity to herpes zoster in older adults.
backHtml: Zoster in older adults reflects waning virus-specific cell-mediated immunity, part of immunosenescence.

frontHtml: Explain how age-related body composition changes prolong the half-life of lipophilic drugs.
backHtml: Lipophilic drugs have a larger volume of distribution and longer half-life in older adults.

frontHtml: Choose a benzodiazepine whose clearance is preserved when phase I metabolism is reduced.
backHtml: When a benzodiazepine is needed in older or cirrhotic patients, choose one cleared by glucuronidation, such as lorazepam.

frontHtml: Distinguish normal cognitive aging from mild and major neurocognitive disorder.
backHtml: Normal cognitive aging slows retrieval and learning but leaves testing within norms and daily function intact.

frontHtml: Describe normal age-related changes in sleep architecture.
backHtml: Aging decreases slow-wave sleep and sleep efficiency and advances circadian phase.

frontHtml: Identify the indication for diabetes screening in overweight adults.
backHtml: Screen adults 35–70 with a BMI of 25 or more for prediabetes and diabetes.

frontHtml: Apply risk-based criteria for statin primary prevention.
backHtml: Offer a statin for primary prevention to adults 40–75 with a risk factor and 10-year risk of 10% or higher.

frontHtml: Recognize when cervical cancer screening is no longer indicated after hysterectomy.
backHtml: Stop cervical screening after total hysterectomy for benign disease without a history of high-grade dysplasia.

frontHtml: Choose first-line management for adult obesity without comorbidity.
backHtml: First-line management of obesity is an intensive multicomponent behavioral intervention.

frontHtml: Apply BRCA risk assessment and referral for genetic counseling.
backHtml: A positive familial risk assessment leads to genetic counseling, then BRCA testing if indicated.

frontHtml: Apply universal one-time hepatitis C screening in adults.
backHtml: Offer one-time hepatitis C antibody screening to all adults.

frontHtml: Select the recommended hepatitis B screening panel.
backHtml: Screen for hepatitis B with HBsAg, anti-HBs and total anti-HBc, which together define infection, immunity or susceptibility.

frontHtml: Choose smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy considering contraindications.
backHtml: Varenicline plus counselling is first-line for smoking cessation; avoid bupropion with a seizure disorder.

frontHtml: Manage a positive screen for unhealthy alcohol use.
backHtml: Unhealthy alcohol use without a use disorder is managed with brief behavioral counseling.

frontHtml: Respond appropriately to a disclosure of intimate partner violence.
backHtml: After disclosure of intimate partner violence, assess safety, document, safety-plan and refer to advocacy; respect autonomy.

frontHtml: Select folic acid dosing for a woman with a prior neural tube defect pregnancy.
backHtml: Prior neural tube defect pregnancy: 4 mg folic acid daily from before conception; everyone else who could conceive: 0.4–0.8 mg.

frontHtml: Apply tetanus wound prophylaxis rules.
backHtml: Dirty wound plus complete series: booster if 5 or more years since the last dose; immune globulin only if the series is incomplete or unknown.

frontHtml: Apply HPV catch-up vaccination recommendations.
backHtml: Vaccinate everyone through age 26 against HPV; start at 15 or older means 3 doses, and no HPV test is needed first.

frontHtml: Identify vaccines indicated after splenectomy.
backHtml: Asplenia: pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY (with boosters) and MenB vaccines.

frontHtml: Apply post-vaccination serologic testing for health-care personnel.
backHtml: Health-care workers need post-vaccination anti-HBs testing 1–2 months after the hepatitis B series.

frontHtml: Respond to a positive depression screen.
backHtml: A positive brief depression screen requires a full diagnostic assessment before treatment.

frontHtml: Provide preconception rubella vaccination correctly.
backHtml: Vaccinate rubella-nonimmune women with MMR before conception and advise avoiding pregnancy for 4 weeks.

frontHtml: Select the vaccines recommended during pregnancy.
backHtml: Give Tdap in every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks and inactivated influenza vaccine during the season.

frontHtml: Apply the one-time nature of AAA screening.
backHtml: AAA screening is a single ultrasound; a normal aorta at 65 needs no repeat.

frontHtml: Select the recommended osteoporosis screening test.
backHtml: Screen women 65 and older for osteoporosis with central DXA.

frontHtml: Recognize and deprescribe an anticholinergic causing cognitive impairment in an older adult.
backHtml: New cognitive decline after starting an anticholinergic drug is an adverse effect: stop the drug before working up dementia.

frontHtml: Choose the evidence-based intervention to prevent falls.
backHtml: For an older adult at increased fall risk from gait and strength deficits, prescribe balance and strength exercise.

frontHtml: Begin the multifactorial falls assessment after a positive screen.
backHtml: A positive falls screen leads to a gait and balance assessment such as the Timed Up and Go, as part of a multifactorial evaluation.

frontHtml: Deprescribe a sulfonylurea causing hypoglycemia in a frail older adult.
backHtml: Recurrent hypoglycemia with a low HbA1c in a frail older adult calls for deprescribing the sulfonylurea and relaxing targets.

frontHtml: Plan benzodiazepine deprescribing in an older adult.
backHtml: Deprescribe long-term benzodiazepines in older adults with a slow taper supported by CBT for insomnia.

frontHtml: Select initial laboratory tests in the evaluation of cognitive decline.
backHtml: Initial dementia evaluation includes vitamin B 12 and TSH to identify reversible contributors, with structural imaging.

frontHtml: Manage urge urinary incontinence in an older woman.
backHtml: Urge incontinence is treated first with bladder training; avoid anticholinergic drugs in older adults with cognitive impairment.

frontHtml: Apply the current adult pneumococcal vaccination schedule.
backHtml: Pneumococcal vaccination for older adults: one dose of PCV20 or PCV21, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23 a year later.

frontHtml: Apply RSV vaccination recommendations for older adults.
backHtml: RSV vaccine in older adults is a single dose, not an annual vaccine.

frontHtml: Apply recombinant zoster vaccine recommendations after prior zoster or live vaccine.
backHtml: Give two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine from age 50, even after prior shingles or prior live zoster vaccine.

frontHtml: Choose the preferred influenza vaccine for adults 65 and older.
backHtml: For adults 65 and older, prefer high-dose, recombinant or adjuvanted influenza vaccine every year.

frontHtml: Apply age limits for colorectal cancer screening.
backHtml: Stop colorectal cancer screening after 85; at 76–85, individualize.

frontHtml: Apply the adequate-prior-screening criterion for stopping cervical screening after 65.
backHtml: Women over 65 without documented adequate prior screening still need cervical cancer screening.

frontHtml: Initiate advance care planning appropriately.
backHtml: Start advance care planning in stable outpatients with capacity by exploring values and naming a health care proxy.

frontHtml: Choose management of frailty and sarcopenia in an older adult.
backHtml: Frailty and sarcopenia improve with progressive resistance exercise plus adequate protein and energy intake.
